#2632. AFC North Roundup: Bengals cruise to division lead; Browns stay in playoff hunt

Even with three teams still firmly in playoff contention, the AFC North race officially has a new favorite, while another team's playoff hopes are all but officially over.

With Cincinnati, Cleveland, and Pittsburgh all multiple games over .500 entering Week 11, there's a very real chance we'll see all three teams in the 2026-27 NFL Playoffs.

As for the Ravens, their latest defeat effectively eliminated them from postseason contention.

Here's a look at what took place in Week 10 for the AFC North.

Cincinnati brought the fireworks. Pittsburgh supplied the audience. With first place in the AFC North at stake Sunday night, the Bengals overwhelmed the Steelers, 38-18, improving to 7-2 with their fifth consecutive victory. Pittsburgh slipped to 6-3 after spending much of the evening trying to keep a divisional showdown from becoming an even bigger embarrassment. The final margin hardly captures how thoroughly Cincinnati controlled the game, which stood at 24-3 by halftime and 31-3 entering the fourth quarter.

Joe Burrow gave Pittsburgh almost no room to breathe. He completed 35 of 44 passes for 409 yards and four touchdowns without an interception, piling up 302 yards and three scoring passes before halftime. Against a defense that had been one of the best in the NFL over the past four weeks, Cincinnati's quarterback repeatedly delivered. The Bengals have now scored at least 30 points in five consecutive games, establishing a franchise record and giving their winning streak some serious offensive muscle.

Ja'Marr Chase was the problem Pittsburgh never solved. His 11 receptions produced 231 yards, including a 53-yard gain that helped set up Cincinnati's second touchdown. Chase Brown caught touchdown passes of two and four yards, while Drew Sample and Dohnte Meyers also scored through the air. That distribution made the Bengals especially difficult to contain: Chase could rip apart the coverage between the end zones, and Burrow had several other answers when Cincinnati reached scoring territory.

The defense made sure Burrow's production came with a comfortable cushion. Cincinnati limited Pittsburgh to 222 total yards and 17 first downs while generating three sacks. Jonathan Allen, Myles Murphy and Boye Mafe each brought down Aaron Rodgers, whose passing line finished at 16 completions in 32 attempts for 145 yards. Pittsburgh managed only a field goal through three quarters, leaving its offense with far too much ground to cover when the touchdowns finally arrived.

Rodgers connected with DK Metcalf and Pat Freiermuth for fourth-quarter touchdowns, but Cincinnati answered the first of those scores with a one-yard Samaje Perine touchdown run. The Bengals finished with a 484-222 advantage in total offense and held the ball for 35:09. Those numbers tell the story of a team that dictated the evening on both sides of the ball.

Deshaun Watson led Cleveland to its sixth come-from-behind victory of the season en route to a 27-24 win over Houston that pushed the Browns' record to 6-4. Cleveland spotted the Texans a 17-0 lead as C.J. Stroud threw early touchdown passes to Nico Collins and Xavier Hutchinson, but the Browns gradually erased the deficit.

Touchdown runs by Deshaun Watson and KC Concepcion, along with a pair of Andre Szmyt field goals, produced 20 consecutive points and a three-point Browns lead entering the fourth quarter.

Houston regained the advantage on Stroud's 11-yard touchdown pass to Dalton Schultz, forcing Cleveland to mount one more rally. The decisive opportunity came with fewer than two minutes remaining and the Browns starting at Houston's 49. Harold Fannin Jr. delivered the biggest gain, taking a reception 30 yards to the Texans' five-yard line. Quinshon Judkins finished the drive on the next snap, scoring with 53 seconds remaining to put Cleveland ahead for good.

The Browns still needed their defense to protect the lead, and Denzel Ward and Donovan McMillon supplied late pass breakups, with McMillon's coming on fourth-and-20 to end Houston's hopes. Cleveland remained unbeaten at home, while the Texans fell to 3-6. The victory kept the Browns within reach in the AFC North and served as a reminder that Cleveland remains part of the divisional conversation.

The Los Angeles Chargers snapped an 11-game losing streak Monday night, beating the Baltimore Ravens 23-20 for their first win of the season. Los Angeles outrushed Baltimore 160-16 and held Derrick Henry to 10 yards on 10 carries. Justin Herbert opened the scoring with a 22-yard touchdown run, and Omarion Hampton scored from the 1 on fourth down to give the Chargers a 17-7 lead late in the first half.

Jacoby Brissett threw for 340 yards in his Ravens debut with Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley both on injured reserve. Baltimore went three-and-out on its first three possessions, but Henry scored twice, cutting the deficit to 23-20 with 10:23 remaining. Herbert finished with 129 passing yards and 51 rushing yards and went without an interception for the first time this season.

The Ravens were approaching field-goal range with 2:03 left when Tarheeb Still stripped Zay Flowers after a catch near the Chargers' 45-yard line. Elijah Molden recovered, and Herbert found former Raven Charlie Kolar for a first down to seal the win. Baltimore dropped to 4-6 with its fifth straight loss that likely ends their slim postseason dreams.

#2629. Kyle Shanahan on the Brian Flores defense: "It's not just a fad"

49ers coach Kyle Shanahan has never beaten a Brian Flores defense. Which might be the most impressive thing that can be said about the Brian Flores defense.

They meet again on Sunday night in Mexico City, when Shanahan’s 49ers play the Vikings, whose defense is coordinated by Flores.

“He’s more unique than all the other 31 guys,” Shanahan told reporters on Wednesday regarding Flores. “He’s the one guy who commits to this and it’s not just a fad for these nine games or whatever. He’s been doing it his whole time in Minnesota. He did the same thing in Miami. He’s as good as it gets at that stuff.

“Anybody who lives in that world as much as he does, it’s usually a matter of time. I think offensive coaches used to like to say that early on, but it’s too many years of it and it’s too many games in this year that they’re sound. They put so much pressure on the quarterback, the play-caller, the O-Line, the receivers, on everybody. A lot of times when you go into an NFL game, the pressure’s really on people on third down and stuff like that because those are things where everything can come and when you play against Brian it’s 70-straight plays of that.”

It’s not easy to beat in part because it’s almost impossible to simulate in practice. As Devin McCourty has said, you think you have a plan and then the game starts and everything changes.

It changes in part because Flores seems to be constantly self-scouting and adjusting, defying the films to create pressure in new ways.

The goal is to eliminate the offense’s built-in advantage that comes from knowing what the play will be by creating confusion for the entire offense. Who’s rushing? Who’s dropping into coverage? Who do I block? If that guy doesn’t rush, what do I do?

It makes for a compelling chess match, with the 49ers needing to find a way to get the Minnesota defense on its heels.

A strong running game is a must. Wearing down the defense physically is required. When inevitable passing situations arise, the quarterback needs to quickly find the open man (if there is one) and get the ball out before the walls close in.

Sometimes, they close quickly. The strategy results in plenty of guys getting a free run at the quarterback, forcing a deer-in-the-headlights response — right before impact.

#2626. Sean Payton won't use Aidan Hutchinson injury as a teaching moment

Lions coach Dan Campbell has made his position clear regarding player celebrations, in the aftermath of defensive end Aidan Hutchinson’s season-ending knee injury. Campbell will not tell his players to stop celebrating.

Broncos coach Sean Payton agrees with Campbell’s position.

“I’m kind of with Dan,” Payton told reporters. “I saw the final comments. We’re teachers and we’re constantly… But we’re going to walk out of the doors, and there’ve been a lot of celebrations. I’m kind of with Dan there where it’s unfortunate. Two good players got hurt on the same play, and I think that there are a lot of other things that I would put on tape on a Friday, Saturday that are [teaching moments]. That I wouldn’t put that on.”

For starters, any non-contact ACL tear quite possibly is the result of a partially torn knee ligament that was on the brink of fully tearing. If Hutchinson’s ACL tear hadn’t happened when he landed after jumping to celebrate a sack of quarterback Drake Maye, it could have happened on the next play. Or the next.

And it’s impossible to expect players to not celebrate. A great play is the product of hours of work and effort and discipline, most of which happens away from the public eye. In the arena, with thousands cheering and millions watching on TV, how can the human beings inside the uniforms be expected not to display human emotion?

Injuries happen in football. The vast majority happen during a play. Some happen after a play. It’s unreasonable to reduce it to none; the players shouldn’t be expected to minimize or eliminate the happiness they experience when everything they’ve done privately culminates in a public moment of achievement.

#2625. Celtics star Jayson Tatum called for technical after throwing ball toward official late in loss to Nuggets

Jayson Tatum got called for a technical foul at the worst time on Wednesday night, and it cost the Boston Celtics a chance at extending the game.

Tatum was called for a technical foul after he threw a ball toward an official in the final seconds of the Celtics' 105-101 loss to the Denver Nuggets at Ball Arena on Wednesday. While the act itself didn't cost the Celtics the game, it made sure they didn't have a legitimate chance to send the contest into overtime.

Denver star Jamal Murray drained a jumper with just seven seconds left in the game, which put the Nuggets up by three points at the time. Tatum caught the ball after it went through the net, and started to make a move to pass it in as the Celtics called a timeout.

But, instead of just turning to hand the ball to the official standing right next to him, Tatum turned and tossed the ball toward the official standing near the scorer's table at midcourt. The ball went behind that official, who seemed a bit confused. The official standing right next to Tatum then called him for a technical foul.

That sent Murray back to the free-throw line. He sank the extra shot, which put the Nuggets up by four and ruined any hopes the Celtics had of forcing overtime.

The throw that Tatum made wasn't egregious by any means. He didn't drill the official with the ball or seem to throw it with any malicious intent. And it even looked like the referee was looking in his direction briefly before turning his back to Tatum once the ball was in the air. Tatum tried to plead his case during the chaotic moments that followed, but the officials weren't having it.

Regardless of intent, throwing a ball at or toward an official like that is often going to result in a technical.

Murray and the Nuggets rallied from an early 15-point hole to beat the Celtics on Wednesday night. Murray had 21 points and seven rebounds in the win, which pushed the Nuggets to 8-5 on the year. Nikola Jokić finished just shy of a triple-double, with 24 points, 9 assists and 8 rebounds. The Nuggets had only 13 fouls called on them all night, compared to the 30 that Boston was hit with.

Tatum led the Celtics with 24 points and eight rebounds in the loss, though he scored only four points in the second half. Neemias Queta finished with 17 points and 10 rebounds. The loss marked the second straight for the Celtics and dropped them to 11-4 on the season.

#2623. Kyle Shanahan on the Brian Flores defense: "It's not just a fad"

49ers coach Kyle Shanahan has never beaten a Brian Flores defense. Which might be the most impressive thing that can be said about the Brian Flores defense.

They meet again on Sunday night in Mexico City, when Shanahan's 49ers play the Vikings, whose defense is coordinated by Flores.

"He's more unique than all the other 31 guys," Shanahan told reporters on Wednesday regarding Flores. "He's the one guy who commits to this and it's not just a fad for these nine games or whatever. He's been doing it his whole time in Minnesota. He did the same thing in Miami. He's as good as it gets at that stuff.

"Anybody who lives in that world as much as he does, it's usually a matter of time. I think offensive coaches used to like to say that early on, but it's too many years of it and it's too many games in this year that they're sound. They put so much pressure on the quarterback, the play-caller, the O-Line, the receivers, on everybody. A lot of times when you go into an NFL game, the pressure's really on people on third down and stuff like that because those are things where everything can come and when you play against Brian it's 70-straight plays of that."

It's not easy to beat in part because it's almost impossible to simulate in practice. As Devin McCourty has said, you think you have a plan and then the game starts and everything changes.

It changes in part because Flores seems to be constantly self-scouting and adjusting, defying the films to create pressure in new ways.

The goal is to eliminate the offense's built-in advantage that comes from knowing what the play will be by creating confusion for the entire offense. Who's rushing? Who's dropping into coverage? Who do I block? If that guy doesn't rush, what do I do?

It makes for a compelling chess match, with the 49ers needing to find a way to get the Minnesota defense on its heels.

A strong running game is a must. Wearing down the defense physically is required. When inevitable passing situations arise, the quarterback needs to quickly find the open man (if there is one) and get the ball out before the walls close in.

Sometimes, they close quickly. The strategy results in plenty of guys getting a free run at the quarterback, forcing a deer-in-the-headlights response — right before impact.

#2617. Tired-looking Lakers can't make their shots in loss to Jazz

The tank appeared to be empty, and there was nothing Luka Doncic or Quentin Grimes could do to help the Lakers this time.

The two had been driving the Lakers during their nine-game winning streak, but the struggles by Doncic and Grimes were a microcosm of what ailed the Lakers during a 109-97 loss to the Utah Jazz on Wednesday night at Crypto.com Arena.

Doncic and Grimes combined to shoot 18 for 48 from the field and six for 22 from three-point range.

Doncic had 29 points, but he was 10 for 28 from the field and two for 12 from three-point range, never able to get on track because of the constant double teams the Jazz sent his way.

Grimes had 20 points, but he was eight for 20 from the field and four for 10 from three-point range.

As a team, the Lakers shot 38.2% from the field and 27.3% from three-point range, with their winning streak going down in the process.

After the Jazz opened an 18-point lead with 1:51 left, Lakers coach JJ Redick waved the white flag, pulling his starters after a rough night.

The Lakers were playing the second game of a back-to-back and for the third time this week, and they looked tired from it all.

The 3-13 Jazz were also playing for a second night in a row, but they won their second straight game despite turning the ball over 23 times.

Read more: How three emergency centers helped Lakers survive the Hornets without Walker Kessler

Doncic was called for a traveling violation late in the second quarter, a call he disagreed with. A few seconds later, he was hit with a technical foul for arguing with the officials.

Early in the third quarter, the Lakers were issued another technical foul, this time on the bench.

It was a tough first half for Doncic and the Lakers. Yes, Doncic had 22 points in the first 24 minutes, but he missed 11 of his 19 shots and seven of his eight three-pointers. He had four of the Lakers' six turnovers.

They shot just 38.3% from the field by the intermission and 26.7% (four for 15) from three-point range.

The Lakers trailed 56-54 at the half despite the Jazz turning the ball over 12 times.

Walker Kessler spent his first four years in the NBA playing for the Jazz, making relationships and friendships that remain even though he now plays for the Lakers. But when the Lakers and Kessler played the Jazz last month in Utah, those same friends did all they could to make life difficult for the big man.

Lakers center Walker Kessler dunks over Jazz guard Ace Bailey in the second half on Wednesday. (Eric Thayer / Los Angeles Times)

Kessler had just two points on just two shots, to go along with seven rebounds. The Lakers won the game, so it was all good for Kessler.

He missed the game against the Charlotte Hornets on Tuesday night with right lower leg soreness but was back starting against the Jazz.

Kessler was looking forward to having a better outing this time against the Jazz.

"I do remember, you know, like, Walker obviously is friends with a number of their players, and they told him, like, 'Our game plan is not allow you to have a single dunk or lob,'" Redick recalled. "So they were really pulled in with that low man, even if the ball was going away from the double-side. In pick and roll, they would tag him with the nail guy as well and pull the low man all the way in. I can't remember the exact number, 47 or something like that, but it was a high-volume three-point game for us. So clearly, you know, an emphasis on taking away those paint points for him. That was the biggest thing from that game."

By the end of the first half, Kessler had just two points, on two made free throws. He was 0 for 2 from the field. He finished the game with 10 points and 11 rebounds but was four for 10 from the free-throw line.

Crosby needs one helper to move past Joe Thornton (1,109) for seventh place on the league's all-time list and is +105 for an assist.

The NHL is not what it is today without Ovechkin and Crosby, and they entered the league together in 2005. They have faced off 100 times in the NHL, including 25 games in the playoffs. In those 100, they have combined for 231 points. A total of 90 games saw either find the score sheet and 49 had both record a point in the same game.

They have met in four postseason series, each in the second round. Crosby and the Penguins won the first three series and won the Cup each time. The Capitals won in 2018 and won their first and still only Stanley Cup. They have played 75 regular-season games in the series. Crosby leads 43-28-4 and has 35 goals and 62 assists in those. Ovechkin has 38 goals and 33 helpers.

The 39-year-old Crosby is in the final year of his contract but has said he has no plans to retire. He and Ovechkin have joined Howe, Alex Delvecchio, Stan Mikita and Steve Yzerman as the only players in NHL history to play 22 seasons with one franchise.

"Over the years, obviously, I've developed a friendship with him and have a ton of respect for him," Crosby said to the media Monday with the Ovechkin news. "It's tough, you come into the league at 18 years old, and before we even met, we were built up against each other."

It should be Logan Thompson in net for Washington, and he was excellent in his season debut in allowing two goals in a win at defending Stanley Cup champion Carolina last Friday. Last season at home, he was 19-9-5 with a 2.18 GAA and three shutouts. Thompson made two starts vs. Pittsburgh overall last campaign and won both with a 1.50 GAA.

The Penguins and Capitals have three meetings left, including Washington's home finale on April 4. That should be quite the Sunday night if both Crosby and Ovechkin are healthy then. Tickets on the secondary market are north of $800 to get in.

The New Orleans Pelicans and Dejounte Murray could be nearing the end of their time together as both sides attempt to find a resolution. Murray has spent the past few years in New Orleans, but there appears to be growing dissatisfaction within the organization.

The guard spent the early years of his career with the San Antonio Spurs. Now, he is reportedly requesting a trade from the Pelicans.

"New Orleans Pelicans guard Dejounte Murray wants a trade from the franchise, and his agent Klutch Sports CEO Rich Paul and team officials have started working on a resolution for the one-time All-Star, sources tell ESPN," ESPN's Shams Charania wrote.

However, finding a trade partner for the defensive-minded guard could prove difficult. Murray is coming off an injury and is currently viewed as a negative trade asset.

"Murray is two years removed from an Achilles tear. He played 14 games last season and is not a three-point threat. He will collect $33 million this season and has a player option for $31 million for the next one. Two team officials I talked to said they would ask for a first-round pick to absorb Murray's contract," Sports Illustrated's Chris Mannix wrote.

Finding a new home for Murray might be difficult, but there could be a potential solution. CBS Sports' Sam Quinn believes the Miami Heat could explore swapping Andrew Wiggins for Murray in a trade.

"The Heat need a more reliable shot-generator than Murray, but after spending most of their assets on Antetokounmpo, their options are somewhat limited. This sort of swap would essentially be a bet that going from one of the NBA's worst organizations to one of its best could rejuvenate a former All-Star. Fitting a point guard that shoots poorly from deep on a Giannis team would be pretty problematic, but Miami would presumably stagger the two of them to limit their minutes together. Such a swap would appeal to New Orleans for a few reasons. The first is contractual. Wiggins signed an unusual contract last offseason," Quinn wrote.

A potential deal would be a significant move for Miami, but there would also be considerable risk in exchanging Wiggins for a player who has struggled to regain his previous form. While Murray was once an All-Star, his recent injury history and offensive limitations could make this a questionable move for the Heat.

Murray is currently playing on a $114 million contract with the Pelicans. He can still provide value defensively, but his offensive struggles could be problematic for a Miami team that has experienced scoring difficulties of its own. Ultimately, the Heat would have to determine whether Murray could provide enough of a boost to justify taking on his contract and injury concerns.

#2613. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2611. Isack Hadjar reveals why he cannot follow Max Verstappen into racing outside F1

Red Bull Formula 1 driver Isack Hadjar says he would love to race in other categories during the off-season, but admits he does not "have enough money" to do so yet.

Several of Hadjar's rivals already race outside grands prix. Red Bull team-mate Max Verstappen has spent 2026 racing GT3 cars, taking part in the Nurburgring 24 Hours in May and the GT World Challenge finale at Portimao, while Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso will take on the Dakar Rally in January.

While speaking to the media ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend, Hadjar was asked whether he had plans of his own to bridge the gap to next season.

"I would love to, but I just don't have enough money to go drive everywhere in the world. It will come one day," Hadjar explained.

"They were not doing this kind of stuff when they were my age. And I'm at a stage of my career where I can't afford doing these things anyway. So, it will come."

The Frenchman said his focus for now was on improving as an F1 driver.

"I'm focused on one thing at the moment, and once I get better at what I do, I'll be able to go out of my zone," he added.

Verstappen and Alonso have both had long and successful F1 careers. Verstappen has also been linked with a Spa 24 Hours entry next year, while Alonso has said Le Mans and the Indianapolis 500 are also on his mind.

Hadjar is in his first season at Red Bull, after stepping up from sister team Racing Bulls, where he made his F1 debut in 2025.

It has been a strong first year with the senior team, despite a wrist fracture that forced him to miss three races. He finished third at the Brazilian Grand Prix and currently sits eighth in the drivers' standings on 122 points.

Hadjar is now targeting his maiden grand prix win before the season ends.

"I'd like to win a race. I have three attempts before we move on to another season. So, I'm going to go all in. I don't have anything to play for. So, I'm just going to have fun, honestly," he said.

He believes Las Vegas could suit Red Bull.

"It's just a feeling I have. I just think this track would suit us more than anything. So that's why it's a good opportunity. But if it doesn't happen, then I just keep pushing," Hadjar said.

#2604. Astros name franchise icon Brad Ausmus as new manager as Houston tries to turn back the clock

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Houston Astros have chosen Brad Ausmus as their next manager, the team announced on Wednesday

Ausmus replaces Joe Espada, whose contract as Houston manager was not renewed after three seasons. Espada led the Astros to the playoffs in two of those seasons.

"I am very excited to be back in Houston," Ausmus said in a statement. "The Astros and the city of Houston have been a huge part of my life, and I'm thrilled to create a new chapter as the team's manager. I'd like to thank [general manager Randy Flores] and the entire Astros organization for this opportunity, and I can't wait to get to work."

Ausmus, 57, had served as bench coach for the New York Yankees since late 2023. Prior to that, he had two stints as a big-league manager. He first managed the Detroit Tigers from 2014-17, and over that span he guided the team to a 314-332 record and a division title in his first season. Ausmus also managed the Angels to a 72-90 record in 2019. Overall, Ausmus as a manager has a winning percentage of .478 in five seasons.

Before his dugout career, Ausmus was a top defensive catcher for years. Ausmus's playing career spanned parts of 18 seasons in Major League Baseball, 10 of which came with the Astros. Along the way, Ausmus won three Gold Gloves behind the mask and earned an All-Star selection as a member of the Tigers in 1999.

"We are thrilled to welcome Brad back to the Astros organization," Flores said in a statement. "Brad impressed us throughout the interview process, demonstrating the leadership, energy, and expertise critical to driving a winning culture both on and off the field. I am excited to work alongside Brad and happy to have him back in an Astros uniform."

With Houston, Ausmus is the first major hire undertaken by Flores, who himself was named to his post earlier in the offseason. The Astros are coming off a division title and a postseason berth in 2026. However, they also finished 81-81 and had a negative run differential. It's an uncertain future, as the Astros have an aging roster in spots, a weak farm system, and multiple core contributors entering their walk years in 2027.

It remains to be seen whether owner Jim Crane will try to wring out another season of contention from the roster or lean into a rebuild. Whatever the course, Ausmus will help guide it in a city where he remains a highly popular figure.

As of Houston's decision to hire Ausmus, the Los Angeles Angels are the only team with a current managerial vacancy. Earlier in the offseason, the Philadelphia Phillies retained interim manager Don Mattingly on a permanent basis, as did the New York Mets with Andy Green, and the Seattle Mariners replaced Dan Wilson with Jason Kanzler.

#2603. Littler shocked by brilliant Wattimena at Grand Slam

Defending champion Luke Littler suffered a shock early exit at the Grand Slam of Darts after a stunning display from Jermaine Wattimena.

The Dutchman was in tears after securing a remarkable, and thoroughly deserved, 10-8 victory in the second round in Wolverhampton.

Having looked imperious as he won six legs on the spin to take a 7-2 lead, 16th seed Wattimena showed signs of nerves as the finish line approached, but dug in to stave off a late Littler comeback and progress to the quarter-finals.

"I think I played really incredible, I played my best game on this stage and I'm really proud of it," an emotional Wattimena told Sky Sports.

"He started playing well at the end. Last leg, [I had] one dart for the match - amazing."

Wattimena finished with an average of 101.70 having hit a staggering 10 180s and, such was his level for the majority of the match, he might feel the margin of victory should have been more comfortable.

The 38-year-old twice threatened nine-darters and had two darts for an 8-2 lead, with Littler rarely even given a look at a double.

However, the 19-year-old world champion sensed an opportunity and showed his class with a 10-darter to break throw as Wattimena finally stuttered a leg from victory.

But a dramatic comeback fell just short as, with Littler waiting to pounce on 65, Wattimena hit tops to take out 77 for the match and reach the last eight of the tournament for a second time.

Wattimena will face compatriot Kevin Doets in the next round after the world number 23 saw off Scotland's Cameron Menzies 10-5.

Doets averaged 101.51 and matched Wattimena's 10 maximums as his relentless scoring made up for an off night on the doubles.

Jermaine Wattimena will face fellow Dutchman Kevin Doets in the next round [Getty Images]

Fourth seed Gerwyn Price is also through after a clinical display to beat Englishman Ryan Searle 10-7.

The Welshman averaged 103.31 and hit 45% of his doubles to see off 13th seed Searle, who himself averaged just under 100.

Price will face Niko Springer for a place in the semi-finals after he overcame former world champion Rob Cross 10-8.

Cross averaged 96.05 to Springer's 88.59, but the German's finishing was far superior - with a checkout rate of 48% - and that proved the difference.

#2601. At MLB GM Meetings, the Phillies are at a crossroads while the Mets have a clear priority

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

LAS VEGAS — The Phillies are at a crossroads. A team that is still full of promise. A team that can compete with some of the best clubs in the league. A team that has World Series hopes. But also a team whose core consists of aging superstars.

"We have a lot of high-end salary players, and they're not young, they're not old, but they're in that age bracket that you have to make a decision," Phillies president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowksi said Tuesday during GM Meetings. "Maybe we have enough high-end players, and we need to complement them with other players overall. That's a decision we have to make."

With a likely lockout looming and the financial structure of baseball's future unclear, the Phillies have a projected payroll of $247 million for 2027. Roughly two-thirds, or approximately $164 million of that money, will go toward players who are 34 or older, including household names such as Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber, and Zack Wheeler.

All three had quality seasons in 2026, but it's fair to question whether this team has reached its ceiling. Wheeler is entering his age-37 season, while Harper and Schwarber are entering their age-34 seasons. That figure above doesn't account for Trea Turner, an aging shortstop who will turn 34 in June, or Aaron Nola, who also turns 34 that month. Turner and Nola will make a combined $51.8 million in 2027.

"Right now we need an outfielder," said Dombrowski. "You're talking about an outfielder, you're talking about some right-handed hitting, a utility infielder, a bit more in the bullpen."

Can Dombrowski do it all? Especially in a market and a game that is defined by uncertainty this offseason?

"I don't know," he said. "It might be hard because they all cost money, too."

Whether it's through free agency, trades, or both remains to be determined. If the Phillies do spend in free agency, Seiya Suzuki remains on the Phillies' shortlist of possible options.

Despite the unpredictability surrounding the 2027 season and Philadelphia's financial commitments to aging players, Dombrowski acknowledged that owner John Middleton remains willing to spend if the right opportunity presents itself.

Still, building from within provided a good amount of the tenor during Dombrowski's media availability. The Phillies' leader was adamant regarding infield prospect Aidan Miller, intimating that the 22-year-old is certainly a real possibility as a key contributor — even more so with the struggles of Turner at shortstop in 2026.

"I really am not going to ever anoint a young player a position," Dombrowski said. "I do think he has the capabilities, and it's just not me. Anybody that's seen him, and people from other organizations probably saying, 'Wow, you still have to earn the spot, but I think that, as it stands, that would be very helpful for us to have that consideration.' And frankly, I'm hoping he does. I'm not giving it to him. But I'm hoping that he does."

A fellow should-be NL East contender is connected to the best free agent on the market.

Left-hander Tarik Skubal will reportedly meet with the Mets next week. The incumbent Dodgers, according to general manager Brandon Gomes, have also been in contact with Skubal. The expectation is that those two sides will meet at some point as well, Gomes said at the GM Meetings Tuesday. While other teams, including the Padres are expected to make a run at Skubal, the Mets and Dodgers are currently viewed as the frontrunners.

The Mets are coming off an abysmal season, finishing at the bottom of the National League East with a 74-88 record. Surely the club is in need of starting pitching, posting a 4.47 rotation ERA, the seventh-worst mark in baseball. David Stearns, the Mets president of baseball operations, elected not to comment on the Skubal sweepstakes, a customary practice this time of year, but spoke around the team's needs.

"Having a complete rotation is really important, and that includes having pitchers who can successfully get you through a postseason and get you through a playoff series," Stearns said. "We've seen over and over again in the playoffs that that can be constructed in a variety of different ways, and so we're open to doing it in any way possible."

Skubal, certainly, would offer New York an anchor to its rotation. An ace that the Mets haven't seen since Jacob deGrom. But he isn't a sudden fix to all of the Mets' pitching woes. Unquestionably, talented depth also stands at the forefront of some of the team's needs.

The club traded Freddy Peralta to the Rays at the deadline after a bad first half with New York. He turned a corner once he got with the Rays and helped lead them to a World Series. Also at the deadline, the club traded Clay Holmes, a converted starter, to the Cubs.

Both pitchers are now free agents. Meanwhile, Kodai Senga and Sean Manaea, two veterans who have underperformed in recent years, are set to become free agents after the 2027 season (Senga has a $15 million option for 2028 that will likely be declined).

Skubal is a logical fit in Queens, especially if Steve Cohen is ready to open his wallet.

"Every situation is unique," Stearns said. "It's been well-publicized, even since I've been here, we've engaged in extremely long-term negotiations for pitchers. We will do so again, but the situation matters. The specific circumstances matter. We do have to look at every individual pitcher on a case-by-case basis."

#2597. Vote for the first BBC Men's Footballer of the Year

Voting is now open for the BBC Men's Footballer of the Year 2026 award, which will be presented at Sports Personality of the Year.

Fans from the UK can vote from the five-player shortlist of Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Rodri and Lamine Yamal.

The vote closes on Friday, 27 November at 09:00 GMT.

The winner of the award - new for this year - will be presented during the live Sports Personality of the Year show on Sunday, 13 December.

Alex Kay-Jelski, Director of BBC Sport, said: "From the drama and excitement of the men's World Cup to the moments that have captivated fans across the domestic and international game, 2026 has given us so much to celebrate.

"Our inaugural BBC Men's Footballer of the Year award is about recognising the players who have made this year so special, inspired fans and left their mark on the game.

"It's a fantastic shortlist, and I can't wait to see who the public choose as our first-ever winner."

The shortlist was selected by an expert panel comprising former international players and some of the BBC's most respected football voices, bringing together a wealth of experience and insight from across the game.

The panel included Cesar Azpilicueta (Spain), Scott Brown (Scotland), Olivier Giroud (France), Shay Given (Republic of Ireland), Hassan Kachloul (Morocco), Lucas Leiva (Brazil), Benni McCarthy (South Africa), Alan Shearer, Ellen White (both England) and Ashley Williams (Wales).

Read more on the five contenders and cast your vote below.

Bellingham made history this summer as he became the first Englishman to score as many as seven goals at a major tournament.

In a superb World Cup for the midfielder, he memorably netted twice in back-to-back games to help the Three Lions beat Mexico and Norway.

That meant he joined exalted company as the first player to score two or more goals in successive World Cup knockout games since Diego Maradona in 1986, and the second youngest in history behind Pele in 1958.

Bellingham also became the youngest European player to make an appearance at four different major tournaments, and also reached the milestone of 50 caps at a younger age than any other England men's player.

The goals continued to flow for Real Madrid, too, with Bellingham notching his 50th for the club to move above the legendary Zinedine Zidane in the Los Blancos' all-time scoring charts.

Bellingham was recently joined in the England squad by his brother Jobe [Getty Images]

In a stunning year of goalscoring, Kane become the first Englishman for 25 years (and only fifth in history) to win the Ballon d'Or - awarded to the world's best footballer.

His tally of 73 goals in 65 matches for club and country during a stellar 2025-26 season has only been surpassed in one of Europe's top five leagues by Lionel Messi's 82 for Barcelona and Argentina in 2011-12.

Kane scored 61 of those goals in just 51 appearances for Bayern Munich as he helped the Bavarians to a league and cup double. His total was 19 more than any other player in Europe's top five divisions.

Already England's record goalscorer, he surpassed Peter Shilton's mark of 125 appearances to become the most-capped Englishman in history.

Six goals at this summer's World Cup also helped him overtake Gary Lineker as the Three Lions' record scorer at the tournament, while he joined David Beckham as the only Englishmen to score in three separate World Cups.

Kane scored his first England goal 79 seconds into his debut in 2015 [Getty Images]

Mbappe came out on top of an enthralling tussle with Lionel Messi at the 2026 World Cup to become the leading goalscorer in the tournament's history.

The France forward, who is still only 27, took his tally to 22 from just three World Cups to finish one ahead of the great Argentine.

Mbappe's 10 goals from eight games this summer meant he won his second World Cup Golden Boot - a feat no player has managed before.

It also made him the first man to reach double figures at a World Cup since Gerd Muller in 1970, with only Just Fontaine (13) and Sandor Kocsis (11) having scored more goals in a single tournament.

Other achievements in a standout year included him finishing runner-up in the Ballon d'Or awards and overtaking Olivier Giroud as France's all-time leading goalscorer.

He scored 25 times to retain his title as La Liga's top scorer during a 2025-26 campaign in which he netted 42 goals in all competitions for Real Madrid.

Mbappe has won eight consecutive league golden boots [Getty Images]

Midfield maestro Rodri earned yet another accolade in his incredible career when he was awarded the Golden Ball trophy for the World Cup's best player.

By captaining Spain to glory in the US, Rodri became only the fourth male player to win the World Cup, European Championship, Champions League and Ballon d'Or - following in the footsteps of legendary Germans Gerd Muller and Franz Beckenbauer and France's Zinedine Zidane.

His achievements were made all the more special given doubts remained over whether he would recapture his best form after a long recovery from a serious knee injury in 2024.

Then Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola predicted he would return to his best at the World Cup and he was right. Rodri completed 756 passes there - the most in the tournament since records began in 1966.

His final season at Manchester City before departing for Barcelona ended in familiar fashion with a domestic cup double taking his trophy haul with the club to 14.

Rodri scored the goal that won Manchester City the Champions League in 2023 [Getty Images]

Lamine Yamal continues to rewrite the record books with his astonishing exploits for club and country.

Just days after his 19th birthday, the Spaniard became the youngest footballer to have played in - and won - both a World Cup and a European Championship. The only players younger than him to play in a World Cup final are Brazil's Pele in 1958 and Giuseppe Bergomi for Italy in 1982.

For the second year running, his performances led to a podium place at the Ballon d'Or and at the same award ceremony he became the first footballer in history to win the Young Talent of the Year three years in succession.

At club level, he was named La Liga's Best Player courtesy of a starring role in Barcelona's title success. The teenager ended the season with an impressive 24 goals and 18 assists across all competitions.

He recently broke Kylian Mbappe's record for the most goals by a teenager in Champions League history.

Lamine Yamal was 16 years and 362 days when he scored at the European Championship in 2024 [Getty Images]

#2596. Corey Seager landing spots: Six possible destinations with Rangers veteran on the trading block

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

A new star-quality trade candidate recently barged onto the scene in Major League Baseball. The Texas Rangers are reportedly fielding and considering trade offers for veteran shortstop Corey Seager.

The Rangers signed Corey Seager to a 10-year, $325 million deal prior to the 2022 season, and that splash signing played a leading role in the Rangers' 2023 World Series triumph. Seager was named MVP of that World Series, and during the regular season he enjoyed perhaps the best campaign of his standout career. Now, though, with the Rangers facing an uncertain future, they may be looking to unload Seager and the five years and roughly $155 million left on his pact.

It won't be simple. Seager is going into his age-33 campaign in 2027, and he suffered a downturn at the plate this past season (while still remaining a plus at the plate and in the field). As well, he's been injury-prone for much of his 12-year career. Over the last four years, he's averaged 111.5 games per season, and in recent times he's been limited by injuries to his thumb, hip, back, and both hamstrings. At his age and after such a long history of health issues, there's no reason to think that will change. Additionally, Seager can control the process. While his contract included a limited no-trade clause that allowed him to block trades to eight teams of his choosing, Seager has now earned "10 and 5" rights – i.e., he's spent at least 10 seasons in the majors and the last five with the same team – which means he has the right to block any trade.

All that said, Seager is no doubt appealing to teams in contending mode and in need of upgrades on the left side of the infield. He still has strong quality-of-contact indicators at the plate, and he's still an asset with the glove. It's easy to dream on that career OPS+ of 135 from the shortstop position and the fact that he was at peak, at least when he was on the field, as recently as 2025. The Rangers are also presumably willing to pay down a chunk of his remaining commitment in order to make a trade more tenable. As for Seager's druthers, it's possible he'd like to play out his contract for a team better positioned to deliver to him a third career World Series ring.

With all those considerations laid out, let's have a look at a handful of teams who may – or at least should – be kicking the tires on a Seager trade. We'll proceed in taut and suspenseful alphabetical order …

The Braves made it to the NLDS this past season and have made the playoffs in eight of the last nine years. For much of that time, though, they've struggled to find a reliable presence at shortstop. This past season, Atlanta shortstops combined to bat just .222/.280/.322, which is squarely in "unacceptable liability" territory. As well, the top two turn-takers at the position, Mauricio Dubón and Ha-Seong Kim, are both free agents.

Boston still has Trevor Story under contract through next season with a club option for 2028. However, Story, who soon turns 34, appears to be very much in decline, and that's in addition to his troubles staying healthy. This past season, he had an OPS+ of just 75 and was barely above replacement level overall. The Sox have signaled they're open to an upgrade at the position, and Seager would certainly be that.

Why not a headline-grabbing reunion in L.A.? Seager was a Dodgers lifer before he inked that big contract with Texas, and that level of familiarity – plus the Dodgers' ongoing excellence – could be alluring. The Dodgers could also use an upgrade in the middle infield. They could install Seager at short and shift Mookie Betts to second base, where he has significant experience. Or they could keep Betts at short, where he's adapted so very well, and let Seager transition to second – a marginally less taxing position that might even help him stay on the field. Tommy Edman, meanwhile, would transition back to a super-utility role. Either way, it's a compelling theoretical fit.

The Yankees have previously shown trade interest in Seager, so it's no great leap to think they still might be eyeing him from afar. Young George Lombard Jr. is the shortstop of the present and future in the Bronx, so Seager would likely need to be willing to shift to third base if a Yankees trade is to come to pass. The Yanks have already signaled they're ready for an upgrade over Ryan McMahon, who's been frankly terrible at the plate since being acquired from the Rockies. The lefty-swinging Seager doubtless would enjoy that short porch in right at Yankee Stadium.

Trea Turner is signed through 2033, but defensively he's become unplayable at the shortstop position. No surprise, then, that the Phillies are open to moving him, perhaps to the outfield, and finding someone else to man the critical position of short. Seager would be a needle-moving addition for lead operator Dave Dombrowski as he attempts to keep the Phils' contending window open for a bit longer. There's an argument that this would make the Philly lineup too left-handed, but the potential upgrade over what Turner provided them this past season makes it a worthwhile sacrifice.

The Jays had one of the worst offenses in all of baseball last season, and that lack of punch was the leading culprit in their tumble from the heights of 2025. Seager could be installed at short or second, and from there the Jays could shuffle infield incumbents Andrés Giménez and Ernie Clement. Indeed, Clement is perhaps at his most valuable when he's deployed as a heavily used multi-positional talent.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2592. MLB rumors: Yankees eye Alec Bohm, Tarik Skubal books more meetings, plus Nationals, Red Sox, Mariners, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The uncertain 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is fully underway. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 1 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22. As for the present moment, the General Manager Meetings in Las Vegas are underway, and since there may not be any Winter Meetings this offseason (thanks to the lockout), the GMs' pow-wow could instead be a locus of activity.

Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace and the ongoing GM Meetings, offseason rumors are flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Wednesday's supply just below.

The Red Sox are once again shopping outfielder Jarren Duran, reports the Boston Globe. He has been in trade rumors constantly the last two years or so. Boston has also reportedly shown interest in free agent Seiya Suzuki, the best right-handed bat on the market. With Gold Glover Wilyer Abreu entrenched in right, the Red Sox would presumably use Suzuki in left field or DH.

Duran, 30, has two years of team control remaining and he's a possible buy-low candidate. From 2023-25, he authored a .276/.339/.471 batting line with 17 homers and 32 steals per season. He slipped to .207/.266/.361 in 2026, however, and the Red Sox need to add power and get more right-handed. Moving Duran to clear a spot for Suzuki would address both needs.

The New York Yankees are eyeing an upgrade at third base given the prolonged struggles of Ryan McMahon, and free agent Alec Bohm may be a potential target for GM Brian Cashman, according to the New York Post. Bohm, 30, is coming off a subpar walk year for the Philadelphia Phillies, but he has a career OPS+ of 101 overall. He also fared much better in the second half, and his season-long numbers were dragged down by a terrible April. Bohm is not much of a fielder these days, but the Yankees may be willing to live with that if they determine he can provide an offensive upgrade.

As for McMahon, Cashman already conceded to looking for a replacement.

"He's signed through next year for us, but I definitely know we need to improve production in a lot of different spots on the club if we can," he told reporters on Tuesday. "So we'll be open-minded to finding what we can run into if it's there."

The market for ace Tarik Skubal, far and away the top free agent available this offseason, continues to pick up steam, and it may be that he signs his next contract before the owners lock out the players on Dec. 1. The Los Angeles Dodgers, who traded for Skubal leading up to the deadline, the New York Mets, the Chicago Cubs, and the San Diego Padres are known to have varying levels of interest in Skubal. Now, the New York Post reports, the Toronto Blue Jays have entered the fray and emerged as Skubal suitors.

As for the Dodgers, they indeed plan to meet with Skubal, GM Brandon Gomes said. There could be a twist in their pursuit, though; The Athletic reports that the Dodgers are interested in Skubal on a short-term deal, presumably with a higher AAV like they gave to Kyle Tucker. But given the uncertainty of the CBA, would Skubal be willing to sign a contract that has him back on the market in just a few years?

Mets top executive David Stearns, meanwhile, emphasized on Tuesday that he and the club are willing to offer lengthy contracts to pitchers but that circumstances matter. That, in theory, should allay fears that he's not prepared to make a significant offer.

The San Diego Padres not long ago declined their club option on right-handed starter Nick Pivetta. However, they may not mean a parting of ways for club and player. Padres lead decision-maker AJ Preller on Tuesday told reporters, including Marty Caswell, that the team hopes to work out a new agreement with Pivetta so that he can return to San Diego for the 2027 season and perhaps beyond. Pivetta enjoyed a standout season in 2025, but his 2026, while excellent while on the mound, consisted of just eight regular-season starts because of elbow problems.

Dylan Crews, the 24-year-old outfielder for the Washington Nationals, has yet to reach the potential that made him the No. 2 overall draft pick in 2023. However, that ceiling is still there, and Crews is obviously young enough to realize his promise. Speaking of Crews, the Athletic reports that multiple teams have approached the Nats about Crews' availability in trade and that the Nats have not declared him off-limits. That of course doesn't mean a trade will happen, but a change of scenery for Crews may indeed be a winter possibility.

Outfielder Randy Arozarena was the Seattle Mariners' top player last season, and now he's a free agent. The M's, though, may not be interested in bringing back Arozarena and instead may be targeting fellow free agent outfielder Seiya Suzuki, the Seattle Times reports. Each veteran outfielder will be going into his age-32 season in 2027, and each produced at a high level in 2026.

After missing the playoffs in back-to-back seasons and trading away catcher Adley Rutschman leading up to the 2026 deadline, the Baltimore Orioles seem like a teardown candidate on paper. However, president of baseball operations Mike Elias batted down talk of a major roster makeover. "A lot of our key, core players are very unlikely to go anywhere," Elias told the media, including the Baltimore Banner, at the GM Meetings.

That presumably means that coveted shortstop Gunnar Henderson, among other notable names, won't be going anywhere this winter.

#2591. Marcus Smart called out for 'fake toughness' after throwing punch at Warriors' Charles Bassey

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Things got heated between the Rockets and Warriors on Wednesday, with Marcus Smart getting ejected late in the third quarter for throwing a punch at the head area of Golden State's Charles Bassey.

Smart and Bassey had gotten tangled up on the other end. After they disconnected and Bassey made his way back on defense, Smart chased after Bassey from behind, made contact, swung around to his front side, and threw the blow that is likely going to lead to a suspension.

MARCUS SMART PUNCHES CHARLES BASSEY 😳 pic.twitter.com/MUsLlDHCz4

What did Bassey do, or say, that got Smart so riled up?

"I just talked to [Smart]. He said they got wrapped up, and [Smart]'s elbow that he hurt got bent up," Rockets coach Ime Udoka explained after the game. "So, [Smart] said something to him. Bassey said, 'What are you going to do?' And he did it."

You can see a better view of the play here.

Looks Like Charles Bassey Had His Arm Tangled Up With Marcus Smart Before The Punch.Nothing Too Serious, Why Did He React Like That? https://t.co/d96UmqUDpM pic.twitter.com/5tmUbokqHR

Smart was hit with a flagrant-2 foul, which carries an automatic ejection (the 13th of Smart's career). Smart didn't stick around long after he threw the punch. As players were being separated to keep things from escalating any further, Smart almost immediately took off his elbow sleeve and walked straight to the locker room. He knew he was gone.

As for Bassey's side of the story, the Warriors' big man said Smart was "playing dirty" all night.

"He's been playing dirty the whole game," Bassey said. "In the first half, I was trying to set a screen and he grabbed my knee. So I mean, he was playing dirty. [On the play in question], I think I was trying to get a rebound and he was grabbing my hand and I was trying to run back on defense. ... And then he got up on me and swung. Obviously that was weak. I think that was, honestly, fake toughness."

Asked whether he said anything to Smart to set him off, Bassey explained: "He said something to me. He said something like, 'Hey, don't do that.' I said, 'Do what?' It's a grown-man's league."

Charles Bassey calls out Marcus Smart for being a fake tough guy and a dirty player 😬(Via @anthonyVslater ) pic.twitter.com/l461taMhtS

As for how long Smart will be out, here's the league's wording on punches thrown from the NBA's official rule book.

So Smart is out at least one game and, again, almost certainly a good chunk of cash.

#2588. No trust problem with Ferrari team - Hamilton

Lewis Hamilton says there is "definitely not" a trust problem between him and his Ferrari team.

The seven-time champion has twice in the past four races ignored a call to pit for fresh tyres, both times to his competitive disadvantage.

The most recent time, in the Sao Paulo Grand Prix on 8 November, Hamilton stayed out on worn slick tyres in worsening rain and ended up spinning before pitting on the next lap.

Before this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, Hamilton spoke positively of his relationship with his race engineer Carlo Santi.

"We're constantly working on our communication," said Hamilton, who had a different race engineer last year.

"It's been a lot better this year. Carlos (sic) has done an amazing job. And those particular two times, particularly the last time, was just I didn't have the information I needed. I got the call right at the last minute.

"We'll just continue to work on the processes. We're super united in what's working, in the right direction."

The previous time Hamilton ignored a call to pit was in Singapore, when he decided to stay out during a virtual safety car period. He later apologised.

At the following race in Austin, he explained that he was "always looking at ways to win, always looking at doing potentially something different. And I wanted to be on a different strategy, not just the same strategy as Charles (Leclerc), where we just follow each other".

Ferrari's Hamilton-Leclerc problem - and other F1 stories to follow

'We've got big problems' - Hamilton says Ferrari need 'serious talks'

Hamilton and Leclerc both insisted that relations between the pair were good after clear-the-air talks in Brazil following a disagreement at the previous race in Mexico, where a tangle on the first lap led to them throwing away a potential one-two and handing victory to Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

Hamilton said in Las Vegas on Wednesday: "Charles is a great driver. The detail we went into about stuff like that in terms of when we close the visor, it's very clear we understand each other.

"We understand each other's boundaries and the ultimate goal, which is to get the best result for the team.

"So I don't feel that that will be a problem going forward. I have no concerns or worries about racing him, and I don't think he does with me either."

Leclerc said: "The discussion went very well. Very, very quickly, after a few sentences already, the tension that was there was not there anymore, and it was all fine.

"We both work in the direction of having that second place in the constructors' championship. The second place in the constructors' is important.

"It's also true that we've got a relatively big margin behind, which doesn't mean we need to minimise that, and we still have to work as a team. But what is really important for me now is to try and win before the end of the season and win the race.

"Everything has been taken out of proportion. I'm kind of used to it now, driving for Ferrari for so many years, but things are very often taken out of proportion.

"Of course, the goal is not always to agree, and that will never happen.

New York Yankees ace Cam Schlittler is the winner of the American League Cy Young Award for 2026. Schlittler was a unanimous selection via the Baseball Writers Association of America balloting, the results of which were announced on Wednesday, beating out Blue Jays ace Dylan Cease and Guardians rookie Parker Messick.

Schlittler's win snapped the run of free agent Tarik Skubal, who won the last two AL Cy Youngs as a member of the Detroit Tigers.

This past season, the right-handed Schlitter in his age-25 campaign put up dominant numbers:

In addition to the above, Schlitter led AL pitchers in WAR with a mark of 7.0, and his ERA+ of 215 also paced his league. That 215 ERA+, which means that Schlittler's park-adjusted ERA was 115% better than the league average, is a Yankees franchise record. Among Yankee qualifiers, only Ron Guidry's 208 in 1978 comes close. Additionally, Schlittler tied for the AL lead this season with an FIP of 2.56, and he struck out 31.4% of opposing batters, which also ranked second in the AL.

Without Schlittler's top-shelf contributions, the Yankees, without franchise slugger and reigning back-to-back AL MVP Aaron Judge for almost 100 games, might have struggled to make the postseason. Instead, Schlittler's excellence at the front of the rotation helped them win 93 games, post the AL's top run differential, and advance to the ALDS.

"Cam had as dominant a season as a starting pitcher can have from start to finish," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said in a statement. "He's shown an astonishing amount of growth since we drafted him, and his success is no accident. Cam has a tireless appetite for hard work and refinement that has allowed his talents to truly flourish. This Cy Young is richly deserved. Cam was the most dominant pitcher in our league and continues to grow into a foundational player for this franchise."

While Schlittler was outstanding as a rookie in 2025, this past season, he increased usage of his sinker and cutter and improved ride on his 98-mph fastball helped him take the next step and become one of the very pitchers in all of baseball. Since Schlittler doesn't turn 26 until February, continued dominance may be on the way.

Schlittler is now the seventh Yankee to win the Cy Young Award. He joins teammate Gerrit Cole in 2023, Roger Clemens in 2001, Guidry in 1978, Sparky Lyle in 1977, Whitey Ford in 1961, and Bob Turley in 1958.

Two days after losing by 51 points to the Golden State Warriors, the New Orleans Pelicans managed an even more embarrassing loss on Wednesday when they were blown out 145-111 by the Brooklyn Nets, who were 2-8 entering the night.

New Orleans (4-8) began the season on a four-game losing streak before bouncing back to .500 with a four-game winning streak, but has now lost four straight again. The concerning part of their recent skid is that the Pelicans have grown increasingly uncompetitive.

In that initial four-game losing streak to open the season, the Pelicans lost by a combined 23 points in the four games. In their last two games, they've lost by a combined 85 points, leaving Zion Williamson with just one word to describe his team's effort.

"Unacceptable," Williamson said, via ESPN. "I don't even have a lot of words. Just unacceptable."

Williamson called out the Pelicans' defensive effort during this latest losing streak, as they've allowed at least 138 points in three consecutive games. The seventh-year star then called for his team to look inward and be honest with themselves about whether they're doing everything they can to help the team win.

"I said nobody likes to lose like this, but if we don't like to lose like this, we have to start with ourselves first," Williamson said. "Look in the mirror and say, did I do what I needed to do for my team? Not individually. Did I do what I needed to do for my team? And then we go from there."

It's never a good sign when a team's star is questioning the collective's effort level and commitment to winning just 12 games into the season. This is when buy-in should be the easiest to get because a team's goals are still right in front of them, but the Pelicans are already showing signs that they will likely spend another season at the bottom of the Western Conference.

That four-game winning streak -- which was somewhat schedule-aided with two games against the woeful Sacramento Kings and Utah Jazz -- feels like ages ago for the Pelicans. If they're going to turn things around, Williamson is right that it starts with accountability from the players, but with some key injuries to Trey Murphy III and Yves Missi, coupled with poor play, this season could get away from New Orleans quickly.

#2583. Verstappen 'trusts' F1 over Middle East decision

Max Verstappen says he "trusts" Formula 1 has made the right decision in pressing ahead with the final two races of the season in the Middle East.

Last week, F1 stood down preparations for a substitute race at Imola in Italy if the events in Qatar and Abu Dhabi could not be held because of ongoing conflicts in the area.

The sport will now conclude the season in the Middle East, unless the situation deteriorates before the Qatar event on 27-29 November and Abu Dhabi on 4-6 December.

Verstappen said: "I trust F1 and FIA to make the right call on that, right?

"I don't have all the intel. I'm not an officer. I just hope that they make the right call on that. And that's all that you can rely on, really.

"They also send over their findings and understanding. So I trust them."

How sporting events are being affected by Middle East conflict

Yamaha will not travel to Qatar for MotoGP race

Verstappen had previously voiced his opposition to ending the season in the Middle East.

"Normally I am happy to go to Qatar and Abu Dhabi, but you know, when there is a war nearby, and if some of the countries are in conflict with each other, then I think we shouldn't go," Verstappen said in September.

The Red Bull driver's fresh remarks reflect a uniform public stance in F1 on the situation, even though there are widespread misgivings among personnel about travelling to the Middle East in the context of the two conflicts in the area.

Last Sunday Iran targeted a US military base in Bahrain with a drone attack for the second time in three days, the latest salvo in the war launched against the country by the US and Israel in February.

And Houthi rebels in Yemen are advancing in their war against the Saudi-backed government of the country.

Missile attacks from the Houthis into Saudi Arabia are threatening that country's chances of hosting the second grand prix of next season, which is scheduled for 19-21 March.

McLaren's Lando Norris said that while he is "fine" with the decision to race, he is concerned about the "big team" behind him.

"I have my friend's wedding in Bahrain next week, so I was planning on going there and then going on to Qatar and then Abu Dhabi," he added.

"But it's not about me. It's a lot more people. It's the fans, it's the team personnel, so the question is for them, more than I would say it is for myself."

Mercedes driver George Russell said he has "no hesitation" in racing and that while he's "sure some people have their reservations" he doesn't "know of anyone who's concerned".

"I know people who live in the region and they said it quite bluntly, if they didn't feel comfortable they wouldn't be there with their families," he said.

"When you look around the world there are a lot of terrible things going on.

"You've just got to trust in the people. If they say it's safe, then you trust in them. F1 aren't stupid and I'm sure there's plans A, B, C, D, etc. So fingers crossed it'll all be fine."

MotoGP, which is owned by the same US group as F1, held a race in Qatar last weekend without problems.

F1, which has significant commercial links with the Middle East, has been closely monitoring the situation and has been advised by security officials and government figures in the Gulf and Europe that the races can go ahead, and there is no official advice against travelling to Qatar or Abu Dhabi.

F1 said in a statement last week that it was still prepared to cancel the two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi if the situation deteriorated.

"If the situation develops negatively in the coming weeks before the events in the Middle East, we will not hesitate to do the right thing and the safety of everyone will always be the priority," an F1 spokesperson said on Tuesday.

The Golden State Warriors' fairytale start to the season got a dose of reality on Wednesday when Stephen Curry suffered an injury to his oblique in a loss to the Houston Rockets.

An MRI on Thursday confirmed an oblique abdominal tear and the team announced that Curry will be re-evaluated in two weeks. While two weeks is the best-case scenario, that being just the re-evaluation point means his absence could extend beyond that timetable -- as that also doesn't include any ramp-up process he would need to clear before returning to the floor.

The injury happened halfway through the first quarter. You can see Curry get tangled up with Alperen Sengun and grab at his side after they separate.

Steph Curry got injured after Sengun grabbed and twisted his arm pic.twitter.com/4p20Rogpeu

Moments later, Curry hit his lone 3-pointer of the game and could once again be seen grabbing at his side after the shot.

Stephen Curry headed to the locker room with an apparent right hip injury. pic.twitter.com/1zVrNz00bH

Curry exited the game at the next dead ball and didn't return. After the game, Warriors coach Steve Kerr said concern about Curry's injury was "high."

"He said he tweaked something in his abdominal area," Kerr said. "He said he's never done it before. ... Concern is high, but I have no idea the extent of the injury."

In recent seasons, the range of recovery times for other notable NBA oblique injuries has varied.

It's unclear how severe Curry's oblique tear is. These are all strains, which is code for a minor tear, but the worst-case scenario would be a more severe one. We saw this two years ago when the Orlando Magic lost both Franz Wagner and Paolo Banchero to oblique tears that kept Banchero out for 10 weeks and Wagner for more than a month.

Any extended absence would be disastrous for the Warriors, who are not equipped to cover for any Curry injury. Curry has gotten off to a scorching start, entering Wednesday averaging 30.1 points per game on 50.3/45.7/98.7 shooting splits with Golden State winning eight straight games for the first time since the 2022 championship season.

But this was always a fingers-crossed situation with an aging roster. Already down Jimmy Butler and Kristaps Porziņģis, and with Brandon Williams and Gary Payton II also on the shelf and wing Will Richard playing through a ligament tear in his thumb, the Warriors have little, if any, margin for any more injuries.

This comes at a particularly tough time for the Warriors, who are entering their most difficult stretch of the season. On Friday, they'll visit the San Antonio Spurs before facing the Dallas Mavericks and New Orleans Pelicans on a back-to-back.

The Warriors have opened up at 8-4 with a top-three offense, but that can go south very quickly without Curry.

Curry is the latest NBA star to face an extended injury absence in the first month of the 2026-27 season. Jalen Williams and Chet Holmgren (Thunder), Anthony Edwards (Timberwolves), Tyrese Haliburton (Pacers), Kawhi Leonard (Raptors), Paolo Banchero (Magic), Jalen Duren (Pistons) and Kon Knueppel (Hornets) are among the players currently dealing with multi-week absences.
