#2467. Re-grading the Giannis Antetokounmpo trade: Why the Heat and Bucks both look much worse now

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Giannis Antetokounmpo will face the Milwaukee Bucks for the first time as an opponent on Wednesday, but it's a game that feels as though it's a half-decade or more in the making. The Miami Heat were a rumored suitor for Antetokounmpo, who played his first 13 NBA seasons in Milwaukee, as far back as the buildup to his possible 2021 free agency, which the Bucks averted by trading for Jrue Holiday and ultimately winning a championship.

The Bucks kept kicking the can down the road. They secured another extension with Antetokounmpo in 2023 by trading for Damian Lillard. They stuck their fingers in their ears and pretended everything was fine when Lillard tore his Achilles in 2025, in the process bypassing the chance to trade Antetokounmpo with multiple years left on his contract when they could have maximized his trade value. In the end, though, Heat president Pat Riley did what he has done so many times before: he got his man.

Now, Antetokounmpo plays for the Heat while the Bucks are in no man's land. We have around four weeks of data on how these teams are going to look after one of the bigger blockbusters in recent NBA history, so with their first head-to-head bout at hand, let's regrade the trade based on everything we now know.

Let's start with the obvious positive: despite age- and injury-related fears, Antetokounmpo is still mostly himself. He is, by both the counting stats and the all-in-ones, playing either at the level of his Milwaukee peak or somewhere relatively close. He has at the very least been a top 10 player in the NBA this season, and you could argue him into the top five. Miami paid an All-NBA price and has gotten an All-NBA player.

There are slight signs of slipping in his age-32 season that merit some examination, though they don't come close to triggering any real alarms. His free-throw rate is lower than it's been since 2018, for instance, but it's still near the top of the league. He's scoring 1.38 points per possession when shooting at the rim -- a very good figure that rates him in the 82nd percentile league-wide, per Synergy Sports. We just judge Antetokounmpo on a curve because he was in the 95th percentile last season and generally hovered around the mid-90s when he was winning MVPs and his 2021 championship.

This is, again, not a significant concern. He's still great, and he's supplementing his rim finishing with significant improvement from mid-range. After shooting below 39% from mid-range over the past five seasons combined, he's above 51% so far this season. We can say pretty safely at this point that the 3-point shot is never coming for Antetokounmpo, so this shot will be his pathway to both aging gracefully and combating the walls he'll see at the rim in the playoffs. If this is sustainable, it extends his prime another year or two and makes him close to unguardable while he remains near his physical peak. Thus far, last year's calf injuries have not recurred.

He's slipped defensively. That's almost undeniable. He contested around nine shots per game when he won Defensive Player of the Year in 2020. He's down to around six this season, and opponents are shooting 6% worse within six feet of the basket against Antetokounmpo than they are otherwise, per NBA.com tracking data. That figure was 20.4% in 2020. The all-in-ones share this basic opinion: still good, no longer great. The tape shows an older player who paces himself defensively. He can still summon greatness for stretches, but he's not in the All-Defense mix seriously anymore.

That brings us to the bigger picture. When you trade as much as Miami did, the question is never just whether the player is good enough to justify the cost, but whether the team is. Heat fans would point to the team's ongoing 8-2 stretch following its 0-4 start to suggest that it was. Count me as a remaining skeptic.

Most of those victories came against either the bottom of the league -- the Kings, the Jazz, they needed overtime to beat the Clippers! -- or injured opponents. No Tyrese Haliburton in the Pacers win. No Jalen Duren against the Pistons. No Evan Mobley against the Cavaliers. No Amen Thompson against the Rockets, playing the second night of a back-to-back. They've faced only two true heavy hitters at full strength, the Lakers and Timberwolves, and they stood no chance against either.

The theory of this team relies on a top-five defense. The offense is simply too reliant on shot creation out of its bigs -- Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo -- to be the leading unit for a champion. The early defensive returns have thus far been discouraging, though in fairness, no team has been unluckier on wide-open opponents' 3s. Even during the 8-2 stretch, they're allowing 48.4 points in the paint per game, a well-below-average figure. Their transition defense is nothing special and they're so-so rebounders. They've hung their hat on turnover-generation, but they're by no means elite on that front. The raw numbers are bad. The truth is closer to fine when you factor in luck. They haven't been great, which is what they need to be.

Part of the problem is that they need to play defensively deficient players -- most notably Klay Thompson and, if he eventually re-earns his rotation spot, Tim Hardaway Jr. -- in order to survive offensively. You can get away with that if everyone else is great. Antetokounmpo has taken a step back. Andrew Wiggins has been a mess. Erik Spoelstra is a defensive miracle worker, but the players here just haven't lived up to expectations. Davion Mitchell has become so important offensively that even he's slipped a bit on that end.

Mitchell's playmaking has been a godsend, and a pretty surprising one in context. The Heat tried and failed to get the Bucks to take Mitchell instead of Kasparas Jakučionis in the trade. There's no telling how bad things would be without Mitchell at this stage, but we're still talking about a pretty limited scorer who nearly doubled his 3-point volume and free throw attempt rate in a single season. Miami probably can't expect him to carry this sort of burden forever. Pelle Larsson is more of a connector than a creator in his own right. Down the line, another guard who can create off of the dribble is probably needed here, especially without a strong Antetokounmpo-Adebayo two-man game forming thus far.

The paths to improvement here are narrow here. The Heat are pressed up against a first-apron hard cap, and they'd need Charlotte's cooperation to amend the protection on their 2027 selection if they wanted to trade even a single first-round pick at this deadline. It's going to take a little while to meaningfully upgrade the supporting talent here, and the rest of the Heat offseason reflected that.

They could have perhaps generated the cap flexibility to retain Norman Powell. They elected instead to let him walk, and when they extended Wiggins, they chose to front-load the deal by using his player option rather than spreading the money out to create more immediate hard cap room. Rather than signing a mid-level free agent to a multi-year deal, they added the older Hardaway on just a one-year contract, presumably to maintain optionality going into next summer.

If Antetokounmpo were 28, this patience might make sense. He turns 32 in less than a month. The time to go all-in around him is now. It's an ironic middle ground that the Heat have put themselves in. Miami could justify the cost it paid for Antetokounmpo only through immediate contention, yet they're slow-playing the roster build in what you would expect, just based on the standard aging curve, to be the best individual season left in his career. It really doesn't make sense to do this halfway.

We're talking about the Heat here. They've made the Finals with less talent than they have now, and they are organizationally opposed to intentional rebuilds. There was never a conversation here about, say, trading Adebayo and starting over as opposed to pushing chips in for someone like Antetokounmpo. But if a few years pass and the Heat don't at least make the conference finals with this core, it's going to be worth wondering if that's the path they should have taken. The early returns here are mixed. The Heat bet their future on a single player. He may be good enough to warrant that investment, but the jury's still out on whether their team actually is.

The Bucks dug themselves an enormous hole by refusing to trade Antetokounmpo when the whole world knew they should have. It was over the moment Lillard tore his Achilles. At that point, Antetokounmpo had two years left on his contract, so hypothetical rental trades would have been feasible. He was younger and he hadn't yet lost a year to calf injuries, so his value was higher. Asset-rich teams like the Spurs and Rockets might have been interested. Had the Bucks moved Antetokounmpo in 2025, they would have gotten substantially more than they wound up getting. Instead, they made the disastrous decision not only to keep him but also to waive and stretch Lillard to sign Myles Turner. Yikes.

When the Bucks finally realized they'd reached the point of no return, Antetokounmpo, as an expiring contract, had complete control of the situation. At least four teams with strong offers were turned away because Antetokounmpo simply wasn't interested in extending with them, according to ESPN. He only wanted the Heat or Celtics. Given those circumstances, the Bucks still managed the negotiations as well as they reasonably could have. They used the Celtics as an effective scare tactic to compel Miami to give up pretty much all of its available draft capital, plus Jakučionis instead of Mitchell.

You can win a negotiation and still lose a trade, though, when most of the things the other team had to give in a trade just weren't that valuable. The big swing piece here was Kel'El Ware, an extremely high-risk, high-reward young big man with star-level raw talent and a pretty iffy reputation when it comes to his motor and commitment. The Bucks, thus far, have gotten the worst version of him. He's playing less in his third season with the Bucks than he did in two years with the Heat despite being on the worst roster of his career. He's missing shots everywhere, his defense has been miserable, and if he's ever going to reach that sky-high ceiling, it's probably going to have to come on his third team.

That, in a nutshell, is the problem here. The Bucks traded the greatest player in franchise history, one of the 25 or so best players the league has ever seen, and got no one who could credibly be considered a cornerstone moving forward. Ware looks like a swing and a miss. It's too early to say much on Nate Ament, but he's a No. 13 overall draft pick, so odds are, he's going to be fine and not much better. Tyler Herro and Jaime Jaquez Jr. are both about what they expected, but both will need to be paid next summer. Herro's presence exacerbates a preexisting glut of guards. His presence has forced last year's breakout guard, Ryan Rollins, to the bench. Maybe that makes him a bit cheaper as a free agent next summer. It also probably sours him on a future in Milwaukee.

Speaking of the guard glut, the Gary Trent Jr. investigation looms large over this trade. The NBA set a notable precedent in the Kawhi Leonard case that it is willing to strip teams of draft picks acquired through trade. This is notable because the Bucks have so little control over their own first-round picks moving forward. The picks they got from the Heat in 2031 and 2033, at least for now, are the crown jewels of this trade. Both of them are theoretically vulnerable if the NBA finds that the Bucks circumvented the salary cap.

It's even worth wondering if the Bucks should or could have used the Antetokounmpo situation as an escape hatch on any preexisting agreements with Trent, if one actually existed. If the Bucks felt an obligation to pay Trent more than the market suggested he was worth, and if they knew they had so many guards that he was unlikely to factor into their rotation (he played less than 40 total minutes before bizarrely leading the Bucks in playing time in Sunday's loss to the Hawks despite coming off the bench), then why not use the leverage Antetokounmpo's availability granted them to foist Trent on Miami through a sign-and-trade? Of course, if the Bucks had the foresight to do this, they probably wouldn't be in this situation in the first place. For now, the investigation is ongoing and we know little beyond the sheer ridiculousness of the contract itself.

The Bucks are 1-13 as of this writing. That, roughly, was to be expected. This was a bad team with Antetokounmpo, so inevitably, removing an MVP candidate was going to make it far worse. But to leave a trade involving a player of that caliber without a single blue-chip player or draft pick is frankly embarrassing.

The Bucks bungled this Antetokounmpo saga for a year, and even if they managed its end stages properly, they'd dug themselves so deep a hole that there was just no obvious way out of it. Now, it seems they may well have made the situation worse with Trent after the fact. This was an organization-wide debacle.

#2466. Meet Arjan Wijngaard, the man with 3,000 classic football kits in his possession

What do you do when you have nearly 3,000 football shirts in your possession? If your name is Arjan Wijngaard, the answer is allocate a room in your house as an exhibition space and log every single shirt in a comprehensive online catalogue.

Recently, These Football Times spoke to Dutch football shirt collector Arjan Wijngaard, the man behind www.voetbalshirts.org and the owner of one of the largest retro football shirt collections not just in the Netherlands but the whole of Europe.

For nearly 25 years, Arjan has been collecting football shirts from around the globe, beginning with an Everton shirt that was given to him as a gift in 1997. With such an enduring reputation, we asked him what drew him to collecting kits in the first place.

“The first question is the most difficult,” he says. “Of course, I liked football in the first place. That is an important thing if you want to collect football shirts. There is no particular reason why I chose shirts, though. Some people choose scarves (I have some scarves as well because if I can’t get a shirt when I visit a stadium or a game, I try to buy a scarf instead). Actually, maybe I’d better have chosen for scarves or pins; they are a lot cheaper and don’t need that much space!”

Take a wander into Arjan’s shirt showroom and it is easy to see what he means. From ceiling to floor, the walls are fitted racks that groan beneath the enormous weight of his collection. The door is an incongruous rectangle of white in an otherwise ubiquitous banquet of colour, while in the window two mannequins stand sentinel in green and blue raiment. It is a veritable sacrarium to shirts – from clubs both grand and meek.

“In general I like to collect shirts from clubs that are not very easy to find,” Arjan explains. “Like lower and non-league, for example, steps 9 and 10 of the [English football] pyramid or clubs from countries that are not known as famous football countries like New Zealand or Tanzania.”

Not that anyone can turn up and take a tour around his showroom, however. Arjan makes extensive use of the internet to display his collection, for he runs a website – wherein he catalogues the shirts by country, club and division – as well as Twitter, Facebook and Instagram accounts all under the banner of Voetbalshirts.org. But what inspired him to begin this online odyssey in the first place?

“There were a few reasons. Firstly, it is to show others what I have. Secondly, for the insurance to prove I had all the shirts if there is a fire or robbery. Also, having my collection online makes it easier for me to see what I’ve already got, especially when I am looking for new ones online and when I am in (fan) shops abroad.”

These are the two main avenues through which Arjan acquires the vast majority of his shirts. Prior to the ongoing global pandemic, he was undertaking around five trips a year to foreign countries in order to expand his collection, with two or three of these visits occurring across the North Sea in Britain. But with flight restrictions hampering his ability to obtain shirts from the clubs themselves, he has made increasing use of the internet.

“I prefer to get them personally from the club shop near the stadium, but that’s not always possible with over 2,700 shirts,” he admits. “Other options are online club shops and, of course, eBay but also groups on Facebook and other collectors here in the Netherlands, abroad and on Twitter. During the years, I have made some contacts all over the world and that is also a fun part of collecting.”

Indeed, Arjan is embedded deep in the football shirt community where he enjoys a prominent and active role as one of Europe’s most dedicated collectors. He presides over a football fiefdom of 6,000 followers across his three social media channels, while his website has attracted in excess of 200,000 visitors. But, he attests, the shirts themselves are not actually the most rewarding facet of being a collector.

“All the things that come with collecting are maybe even nicer than having the shirts. The visits to the stadiums, searching online, getting in contact with people, meeting other collectors and also volunteers that are proud of their club and want to help me to add a shirt or their club to the collection is great. Shirt collecting got me a lot of positive things besides the shirts themselves. Lots of talking about shirts and football and helping each other through our mutual passion of football shirts.”

As much as the community benefits are enjoyable, Arjan must have a favourite shirt, so we press him for an answer, hard as it may be to choose just one from 2,800 options. “There is one old FC Groningen shirt that is a favourite,” he admits at last, “because it is a rare one, matchworn and almost 40 years old.”

Such a rare and antique shirt is the pride of his collection and, like most of his garments, Arjan refuses to wear it for recreational purposes, although not necessarily for the reason most people might expect. “I tend not to wear my shirts because not all of the shirts are in my size (anymore)!” he says. “I don’t wear football shirts very often. I don’t want to damage them. But, actually, some I have double: one for the collection and one to wear.”

Even with such an extensive and valuable collection, Arjan still has his sights on expanding it further, even though his showroom appears to have reached the point of saturation. Even the door bears host to a number of caps hung on pegs hammered into the wood. He has a shortlist of kits he is working through and he reveals to us the one shirt he covets above all others.

“There is one shirt I really want to add to my collection, a matchworn Groningen cup final shirt from 2015. Groningen is my local team and they only won one trophy. The Dutch cup. And as I said before, I like shirts from non-league clubs I don’t have yet. So, if there are people who are reading this and think they can help me with a shirt from their local non-league club, don’t hesitate to contact me!”

Situated as he is in the Netherlands’ north-east, Arjan’s local team and the one he professes to support most keenly is Groningen, best known in recent years for being the boyhood club of Arjen Robben. It was a love affair that began around 30 years ago and which served as something of a gateway into his lifelong affinity for the sport and the kits associated with it.

“Groningen is my local team. I have had a season ticket for almost thirty years and the stadium is only ten minutes away by bike. My opinion is that you always have to support your local team. But Everton was my first shirt. I guess I like to support people’s clubs. Everton, Groningen and Feyenoord really are people’s clubs.”

Though the boom in shirt collecting has been a relatively recent phenomenon, and one which was no doubt exacerbated by a lockdown that allowed people to invest more time and money in starting or expanding their collections, Arjan has been active on Twitter since 2010. He is, for all intents and purposes, one of the old guard, but what does the future hold?

“I have no plans to stop!” he confesses. “As long as I like it and have the space to continue, I shan’t stop.”

#2465. Agent's Take: Breaking down Dolphins' historic dead money and where they go from here

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

NFL teams have become increasingly comfortable with significant amounts of dead money, meaning salary cap charges for players that are no longer on a team's roster. Just look at the Miami Dolphins.

Under general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan and head coach Jeff Hafley, who were both previously with the Green Bay Packers before being hired in January, the team is taking dead money to an extreme. The new regime has an unprecedented $188.88 million in dead money as of Week 10's loss to the Indianapolis Colts.

However, there's a method to Sullivan's madness as the Dolphins are in teardown mode after a 7-10 record in 2025 with a high-priced roster.

Miami's $188.88 million is easily the most dead money in NFL history for a league year. The record-breaking amount has put the Dolphins at a distinct financial and competitive disadvantage, so it's no surprise that Miami is in a three-way race with the Los Angeles Chargers and the Tennessee Titans for the first overall pick in the 2027 NFL Draft. Each team has a 1-8 record.

So where does Miami go from here with its mess of dead money? Let's dive in.

Miami's $188.88 million in dead money is on par with the league-wide salary cap in 2019, which was $188.2 million (the current salary cap is $301.2 million). Each team's actual salary cap (known as the adjusted salary cap) typically differs from the NFL's set amount because unused cap room can be carried over from one year to the next, and other adjustments can further increase or decrease cap space.

The Dolphins have a $308.878 million adjusted salary cap for 2026, and dead money takes up an unheard-of 61.15% of that number. Just under $120 million in cap space is available for the actual roster, thanks to dead money. Essentially, the Dolphins are building a team this year under salary cap constraints from 15 years ago — the league-wide salary cap was $120.375 million in 2011 following 2010's uncapped year.

Most of Miami's dead money comes from just a handful of players. The Dolphins have four of 2026's biggest dead-money charges from the following players (league ranking is in parentheses):

Inside Tua's dead money: As expected, the new regime went in a different direction at quarterback. Tagovailoa was benched and demoted to third-string quarterback by former Dolphins head coach Mike McDaniel after 14 games last season. He had three years remaining on the four-year, $212.4 million contract extension averaging $53.1 million per year, signed in July 2024, when he was released in March with a post-June 1 designation.

The total dead money for parting ways with Tagovailoa is $99.2 million, a record for dead money associated with a single-player contract. The post-June 1 designation allows the Dolphins to take Tagovailoa's $99.2 million of dead money over two years, 2026 and 2027. Only the current year's prorated bonus amount counts toward the cap for players released with a post-June 1 designation. The acceleration in future contract years is delayed until the following league year (2027 in this case), which will begin next March 11.

The dead money for Tagovailoa is so much because his $54 million base salary (for 2026) was fully guaranteed. Now, prior to his release, the Dolphins decided to avoid his 2026 dead money from reaching $67.4 million. The team exercised an option for a dummy/voiding 2030 contract year by making a $15 million payment (i.e., an option bonus). Once it did so, the option bonus was prorated to $3 million annually against Miami's salary cap from 2026 through 2030. The dead money charges would have been $67.4 million in 2026 and $31.8 million in 2027 if the option had not been exercised, instead of the actual $55.4 million and $43.8 million.

The Dolphins got minimal cap relief from releasing Tagovailoa. His 2026 cap number was $56.3 million, freeing up $867,647 of cap space.

The $55.4 million in 2026 is a record for dead money tied to an individual player in a single league year. It's also a little over $7 million more than 2026's highest cap number, held by Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford at $48.3 million.

Tyreek Hill: Next up was Hill. His $51.1 million 2026 cap number was untenable even before the gruesome left knee injury he suffered early in the 2025 season. Hill was released before a $5 million roster bonus was due on the third day of the 2026 league year (March 13) and $11 million of his unsecured $29.9 million 2026 base salary became fully guaranteed. That resulted in $22.9 million in 2026 cap savings.

There's only one 2026 wide receiver cap hit bigger than Hill's: Chris Godwin's $33.7 million with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Jaylen Waddle: Waddle and a 2026 fourth-round pick were dealt to the Denver Broncos for a 2026 first-round pick (30th overall), a 2026 third-round pick, and a 2026 fourth-round pick. The Dolphins escaped the three-year, $84.75 million extension, which made Waddle the NFL's highest-paid No. 2 wide receiver at $28.25 million per year upon signing in June 2024. The Dolphins lost $11.60 million of 2026 cap space from trading Waddle, considering he was counting $11.63 on Miami's books before he was dealt.

Jalen Ramsey: Ramsey's $20.9 million comes from a June 2025 trade with the Pittsburgh Steelers, where the Dolphins acquired safety Minkah Fitzpatrick and a 2027 fifth-round pick for him, tight end Jonnu Smith, and a 2027 seventh-round pick. Since the trade occurred after June 1, the prorated bonus amount from Ramsey's 2026 through 2028 contract years became 2026 cap charges.

These four players combined account for just under $127.5 million of the dead money. That's slightly over two-thirds of the Dolphins' total amount.

The Dolphins have three other dead-money charges over $10 million: safety Minkah Fitzpatrick ($13 million), edge rusher Bradley Chubb ($11 million) and offensive tackle Terron Armstead ($10.7 million). Collectively, those seven players are responsible for a little less than $162.5 million (or 86%) of Miami's dead money.

The only significant cash from Miami's dead money is Tagovailoa's. That's $52.9 million rather than $54 million because his salary guarantee has an offset clause allowing the Dolphins to reduce the money owed to him. It's reduced by the one-year contract he signed with the Atlanta Falcons at his $1.215 league minimum salary. The other six major dead money charges are just prorated bonus amounts.

The Dolphins made one important free-agent acquisition with their limited budget. The new regime signed Malik Willis, who was Green Bay's backup quarterback to replace Tagovailoa. Willis signed a three-year, $67.5 million contract with $45 million fully guaranteed in March. At $22.5 million per year, Willis is quite affordable for a starting quarterback, although he is the Dolphins' highest-paid player.

The 2025 average salary for starting quarterbacks, excluding those on rookie contracts which are strictly determined by draft position, was slightly over $44 million per year according to NFLPA data. Willis' 2026 cap number is $5.7 million.

There was some speculation that Willis could be benched before landing on injured reserve with a groin injury from Week 9's loss to the Detroit Lions. Surgery may be required, which would likely end Willis' season.

The Dolphins have 14 players on one-year contracts this season. The largest is tight end Greg Dulcich's worth $3.25 million. The other 13 are at or slightly above league minimum salary.

The teardown didn't preclude the Dolphins from extending the contracts of key veteran players. Sullivan identified running back De'Von Achane, center Aaron Brewer and linebacker Jordyn Brooks as three pillars for the rebuild.

Achane signed a four-year, $64 million extension with just over $27 million of guarantees. He is the NFL's sixth highest-paid running back at $16 million per year. Achane, who earned Pro Bowl honors in 2025, is out for the season with a torn left ACL suffered in Week 3.

Brewer signed a three-year, $52.5 million extension with $31.75 million of guarantees, making him the league's third-highest-paid center at $17.5 million per year. He was a named second-team All-Pro last season.

Brooks received a three-year, $48 million extension with $35 million of guarantees. At $16 million per year, the 2025 first-team All-Pro is the NFL's sixth highest-paid off-ball linebacker.

The 2026 cap numbers for these deals are modest, with none exceeding $6.18 million. The Dolphins only have one 2026 active cap number above $10 million. It's defensive tackle Zach Sieler's $11,011,200.

The Dolphins have the league's youngest roster. The average age right after the preseason roster cutdown to 53 players was 25.3 years old, according to Joe Schad of the Palm Beach Post.

A 13-player draft class is helping to lay the foundation for the future, and all but two are on the 53-man roster. Six of the draft picks are starters (three on offense and three on defense). Kayden Proctor, this year's 12th overall pick, has switched positions from offensive tackle at Alabama to left guard in the NFL. He could be moving to right tackle next year since Austin Jackson is in a contract year. Three of the top four wide receivers are rookies, with third-round pick Caleb Douglas leading the way.

Second-round pick Jacob Rodriguez is an NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year candidate. Cornerback Chris Johnson, the 27th overall pick, is starting to make plays more consistently after a rough start to the season. Safety Michael Taaffe, a fifth-round pick, is tied for the lead among rookies with three interceptions.

There is light at the end of the tunnel from a salary cap standpoint. The dead money drops considerably in 2027 to $57.3 million. It primarily comes from the two post-June 1 designations, with Tagovailoa and Chubb accounting for $43.8 million and $12.9 million, respectively. More importantly, the Dolphins have the NFL's fewest 2027 cap commitments at $212.5 million, with 41 players under contract and $4.54 million in existing 2026 cap space that can be carried over to the 2027 league year, according to NFLPA data.

Joel Corry is a former sports agent who helped found Premier Sports & Entertainment, a sports management firm that represents professional athletes and coaches. Prior to his tenure at Premier, Joel worked for Management Plus Enterprises, which represented Shaquille O'Neal, Hakeem Olajuwon and Ronnie Lott.

#2464. MLB rumors: Tarik Skubal hosts more meetings, Red Sox add backup catcher, plus Padres, Phillies, Rays, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The hot stove is starting to heat up. On Tuesday, David Bednar and Ryan Jeffers accepted the $23.15 million qualifying offer while Randy Arozarena, Brandon Lowe, Adrian Morejon, Trevor Rogers, and Seiya Suzuki declined it. Those five are now attached to draft pick compensation. Also, the White Sox landed righty Dustin May on a three-year contract.

We're still waiting on the offseason's first real blockbuster but things are beginning to pick up. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Wednesday's hot stove happenings.

The Red Sox have acquired catcher Nick Fortes from the AL East rival Rays for 17-year-old minor-league righty Angel Roa, the team announced on Wednesday. Fortes will take over as Adley Rutschman's backup catcher. He is projected to make $3.4 million or so through arbitration in 2027, which is a pricey sum for a backup catcher, particularly for a small payroll team like the Rays. Connor Wong has been designated for assignment by the Red Sox in a corresponding move.

Fortes, 30, had a career-best season at the plate in 2026, though his defensive numbers took a big dip. The Rays acquired Liam Hicks at the trade deadline and he is their clear-cut starting catcher. Kenny Piper, who made his MLB debut in August, could step in as the backup until top prospect Caden Bodine is ready, which could be as soon as next summer.

The Blue Jays and Dodgers had in-person meetings with top-ranked free agent Tarik Skubal on Tuesday, reports ESPN. He will meet with the Padres later this week and already met with the Mets on Monday. Rival executives expect it to come down to Blue Jays and Mets, per ESPN. Toronto has a history of pursuing top free agents but missing out (Shohei Ohtani, Kyle Tucker, etc.).

Skubal is expected to sign before the lockout and is therefore working on a tight schedule, much tighter than usual for top Scott Boras clients. The Dodgers are said to have interest in a short-term contract with a large annual salary, something that is unlikely to appeal to Skubal. He's poised to land a record contract for a pitcher, perhaps even more than $400 million.

Star shortstop Corey Seager has expressed an openness to a trade to only a "handful of teams," reports ESPN. Seager has a full no-trade clause and can pick his destination, and was reportedly quite picky as a free agent five years ago. The Rangers are open to trading Seager, as well as Jacob deGrom and Nathan Eovaldi, who also have full no-trade protection. deGrom already reportedly invoked his no-trade clause at last season's deadline to spike a deal to the Braves.

Seager, 33 in April, had surgery to remove a bone spur from his elbow last month, and was limited to 102 games by injuries in 2026. When healthy, he has typically beibeeng very good, but the injuries and surgeries are mounting. Seager is owed $31 million annually through 2031. Texas would likely have to eat some money to facilitate a trade.

On Tuesday, the Padres hosted free agent outfielder Seiya Suzuki for a recruiting visit, according to ESPN. San Diego aggressively pursued Suzuki when he initially came over from Japan five years ago, but he opted to sign with the Cubs instead. We ranked Suzuki as the seventh-best free agent available this offseason, and the third-best free agent position player.

San Diego needs rotation help more than anything this offseason, though they could use another middle-of-the-lineup bat as well. They could sign Suzuki, plant him in right field, and move Fernando Tatis Jr. back to the infield, where he played 53 games at second base this past season. It was Tatis' first action on the infield since he was the team's starting shortstop in 2021.

After signing Jake Bauers, president of baseball operations Craig Breslow said it is "hard to envision that there's something significant on the horizon" for the Red Sox, according to the Boston Globe. That doesn't mean the Red Sox won't do something significant later in the offseason, perhaps after the lockout, but, right now, there is nothing major in the works.

Breslow's next order of business is unclogging his outfield/DH logjam, which could involve trading or even non-tendering Jarren Duran. The Red Sox also have four pitchers for the No. 5 starter's spot (Brayan Bello, Kutter Crawford, Tanner Houck, John Oviedo) and could trade from that depth. Otherwise, Boston has no glaring roster issues remaining this offseason.

Free agent slugger Randy Arozarena is seeking well over $100 million and could end up waiting until after the lockout to sign, according to ESPN. For now, teams are balking at that asking price, but that isn't unusual this early in the offseason. The Orioles and Yankees are among the clubs reported to have interest in Arozarena, our ninth-ranked free agent.

Although Arozarena had the better 2026 season, Suzuki is considered the more desirable free agent because he's a much better defender. They're roughly the same age and are comparable hitters, but Arozarena is a borderline DH at this point. Right-handed power is in shockingly short supply, though. He (and Suzuki) would improve almost any lineup. As noted above, both players declined the qualifying offer from their respective teams, which means they are tagged with draft pick compensation.

The Phillies are receiving trade calls about righty reliever Orion Kerkering, reports The Athletic. Kerkering struggled badly in the second half, allowing 25 runs and 43 baserunners in his final 19 ⅓ MLB innings of the season. The Phillies optioned him to Triple-A a week before the end of the regular season and did not carry him on their Wild Card Series roster.

Still only 25, Kerkering has a history of missing bats at a high level and experience in late-inning situations. He will remain under team control through 2029. The Phillies certainly don't have to trade him. They could keep him and even send him to Triple-A next season. It never hurts to listen, however, and other teams presumably see Kerkering as a buy-low candidate.

Veteran righty Frankie Montas hit 98 mph and wowed scouts during a workout in Arizona this week, reports The Athletic. Multiple general managers were in attendance, and it's possible Montas will land a guaranteed major-league contract. He is rehabbing from Tommy John surgery and has not pitched in an MLB game since August 2025.

Pitching is always in demand, especially cheap pitching with upside behind league-average innings. Montas, 34 in March, has not been healthy and effective at the same time since 2022, though he looked good during his showcase and he has a reputation for being an excellent teammate who mentors young pitchers. That will only help his case.

#2462. Lokomotive Leipzig, the 1987 Cup Winners’ Cup final and a rebirth from the ashes

Picture the scene. A communist-era colossus of a stadium, the vast expanse of concrete stretching as far as the eye can see, enclosing a seething mass of humanity, congregating in their blue and yellow scarfs. They will need them tonight, for this open bowl is completely at the mercy of the elements. The fans do not care, however. This is the Zentralstadion in Leipzig and it is about to witness its finest hour.

They have seen bigger crowds than this here, of course. The Turn-un Sportfest, the socialist government’s regular celebration of athletic achievement, can draw attendances of 100,000 or more. This is the largest crowd it will ever see for a football match, though – and that matters.

Football is the one thing that the authorities cannot control, the rebellious child of the model socialist state. Football fans are not to be trusted; their first loyalty is to their teams and not to the party or the nation. They are prone to singing dissident songs and to bouts of hooliganism. Their unique culture is something that the state will never even try to understand. In these last years of the GDR, the terraces are also at the forefront of rebellion and change, operating, along with the church, as an open cover for opposition to one-party rule, hiding their protests in plain sight.

They will say there were 74,000 people inside the Zentralstadion that night, but many more will claim to have been there. It seems apparent to even the most casual observer that the real attendance is close to touching six figures. Later estimates put the actual number at 120,000.

For the players who are about to step into this febrile atmosphere, this is their chance to make history. Lokomotive Leipzig are on the verge of reaching their maiden European final. They lead Bordeaux 1-0 from the first leg in France and now they stand 90 minutes away from the Cup Winners’ Cup final in Athens.

Lokomotive, the club, had already been through many incarnations. Their ancestors, VfB Leipzig, were the first national champions way back in 1903, when Germany was a unified nation. It is not apparent to those inside the ground tonight, but it soon will be again.

Leipzig start the game with energy, flying into tackles, clearly fired up by the noise and passion of the crowd inside the stadium. It is Bordeaux, though, who take the early lead and go on to control the match.

The home side continue to hold their own, however. They even have a chance to win the game late in the second half but Uwe Zotzsche’s penalty is saved by Dominique Dropsy in the Bordeaux goal. Extra-time is a tight affair and the match drifts to penalties.

Leipzig goalkeeper René Müller saves from Phillipe Vercruysse but Lok’s joy is short-lived as Matthias Liebers promptly sees his kick saved by Dropsy. Both teams’ penalty taking is unerring from that moment on, taking the shootout to sudden death. The tension in the ground is unbearable as Zoran Vujović steps up with the score tied at 6-6. His earlier goal has taken the tie this far but now he looks gripped by nerves.

He hesitates twice on his long run-up before scuffing his penalty straight at Müller. The Zentralstadion erupts: Lok are now one kick from glory. Incredibly, the man stepping forward to take the crucial penalty is none other than Müller himself, the goalkeeper who now has the chance to score the most important goal in his club’s history.

Müller places the ball and starts his run with a determined look in his eyes before blasting his penalty high into the roof of the net. He wheels away, arms in the air, and is instantly mobbed in a sea of exultant teammates.

There is something symbolic about the celebrations inside the stadium. The fans don’t know it but this is as good as it will get for GDR football. Within two years, protests will begin in this very city, as young people craving the freedom of expression of Western society crowd onto the streets that surround the Zentralstadion. These protests will spread all over the nation, culminating in the fall of the Berlin Wall on a cold November evening. Within four years, the GDR will be no more.

So what became of Lokomotive Leipzig and those men in yellow and blue shirts? The team itself would go on to lose the Cup Winners’ Cup final to a dynamic Ajax side containing Marco van Basten, Frank Rijkaard and a young Dennis Bergkamp.

In many ways Lokomotive’s fate since that April night in 1987 mirrors that of the former GDR. Desperate to throw off the negative associations of communism and to seem at one with their new western countrymen, the team ditched the name Lokomotive in 1991 to become VfB Leipzig once again. A brief foray into the Bundesliga followed three years later before the economic reality of eastern life in the united Germany bit hard. By 2004, the club that had stood on the brink of European glory a mere 17 years earlier had ceased to exist.

The old Zentralstadion was a ruin, housing a shiny new ground inside its crumbling bowl. The new stadium was used during the 2006 World Cup in Germany and is now the home of RB Leipzig, the controversial franchise club owned by the Austrian soft drinks giant Red Bull. As an image of capitalism’s utter triumph over communism, only the McDonalds that now stands on Checkpoint Charlie is more symbolic.

For many cities, this may have been the end of their famous old football club, but Leipzig is no ordinary place. The club’s fans rallied round and restarted Lokomotive Leipzig in the 11th tier of German football in time for the 2004/05 season. Fans rebuilt the club’s Bruno-Plache Arena brick by brick with their bare hands until it was fit to host football again.

The response from the city was incredible. Lokomotive even broke the record for a lower-league football match in Germany when 12,421 spectators turned out for a game against Eintracht Grosbenden. The venue for this game? None other than the famous old Zentralstadion itself. The club that refused to die had come full circle.

It would be painting an unnecessarily rose-tinted picture to pretend that everything has been plain sailing since then. Leipzig’s tendency to be a microcosm of the eastern half of Germany has continued as the years have progressed. Lokomotive have not been alone in battling neo-Nazi hooligan elements as the far-right has sought to exploit the economic troubles and resentment of the former GDR for its own ends.

The club has also failed to break out of the regional leagues despite plenty of near-misses over the last few years. However, the current picture is beginning to look altogether brighter. Leipzig is now an up-and-coming city, boasting a thriving tourism industry, trading in both shiny new architecture and GDR kitsch, or Ostalgia as it is called by locals.

Lokomotive, too, are on the up. The club has made commendable efforts to drive out the hooligan element and to make the Bruno-Plache a more welcoming environment for everyone. They boast one of their most impressive squads in recent years and harbour real hopes of soon returning to the Bundesliga structure.

Many lower league clubs have struggled to survive the empty stadiums, or “ghost games” as they are called in Germany, which have become a sad necessity of the COVID-19 pandemic. Lokomotive had their own unique solution to the problem. The club announced they would be selling tickets for €1 to a virtual game against the “invisible opponent” to raise money to pay the club’s 300 staff.

The aim was to set a new club attendance record, beating the 120,000 that were estimated to have been at the Zentralstadion for the Cup Winners’ Cup semi-final. Incredibly, Lok ended up selling 150,000 tickets for this imaginary game, the money keeping the club afloat through the months that followed. They do things differently in this unique city.

The joy of fans returning to stadiums this season has sadly been curtailed recently in the state of Saxony, where Leipzig resides, with matches temporarily being played behind closed doors once again. As a result, the Bruno-Plache Arena currently stands empty. Its last game with spectators was the derby against Chemie, another famous name from the GDR days. Lok won 1-0 in front of 6,000 passionate fans.

Those fans may be absent at the moment but soon they will return to cheer on the men in yellow and blue shirts, for nothing can quell their devotion. To this day, they still tend to their beloved stadium, picking weeds out of its’ cracks and painting its seats. It might not quite be the Zentralstadion on that magical night in 1987, but Lokomotive Leipzig and their fans are home again. Who knows, they may have a few more glory nights left in them yet.

#2459. Edmundo: O Animal

Originally featured in the sold-out Brazil magazine, support high-quality, wholly independent journalism by ordering our magazine. It’s what keeps everything online free.

A cauldron full of seething excitations: that’s how Sigmund Freud describes the id, the psychological structure responsible for our base desires. The id, Freud argues, must be kept in check to prevent man from acting impulsively against his own interests. A failure to repel one’s instincts, he warns, can have devastating consequences, not only for man but also his contemporaries. Nobody in football knows this more than Edmundo.

His legend, like so many others of Brazilian football, began in the exacting slums of Rio de Janeiro. Teixeira de Freitas Street may be just 30km from Ipanema, but for the downtrodden inhabitants of Niterói, it may as well be 3,000.

Whilst the Maracanã glistened across Guanabara Bay, Reinaldo de Souza was trying to raise a family. A barber like his father and brother before him, he struggled to make ends meet whilst his wife worked long hours as a cleaner. With nothing to distract them from the long period without their parents, brothers Edmundo and Luizinho passed their time like any other child in their street. Football became their home, and the pickup games on the beach became their education.

It was just as well for Edmundo, who showed no interest in academia. “Dinho”, as he was known to his family and friends, was focussed on one thing and one thing only. Even at a young age his talent was evident, a diminutive dribbler with a charring swagger, whose talent with the ball was matched only by the sharpness of his temper. He knew he was good and he wasn’t shy about it.

It was his aunt who first spotted his talent. Maria had taken to minding the boys whilst their parents worked, and she would ferry Edmundo to practice and back as well as into the city to watch his beloved Vasco. It wouldn’t be long, though, before he graduated from fan to the first team. Aged 15, Edmundo was invited to trial with Botafogo’s youth wing. Fogão coach Tinoco knew genius when he saw it, and the youngster left Teixeira de Freitas behind for the big time.

It’s at this point in the story where the prodigy defies the odds to succeed. But Edmundo’s tale isn’t one of romance or glamour, and it was at Botafogo that his nascent talent for self-destruction first became evident. With Maria struggling to afford the transport to and from the Botafogo facilities, Edmundo moved into the club’s youth lodging, but barely after joining he was expelled for walking naked through the grounds.

Luckily, Vasco didn’t mind exhibitionists. Perhaps they were swayed by an astonishing goal Edmundo had scored in a youth game in August 1991, where he had slalomed past an entire defence and goalkeeper before depositing a casual finish into an unguarded net.

After impressing for the reserves, Vasco coach Nelsinho gave him his debut in January 1992. The result, a 4-1 rout against Corinthians, augured well for a season in which the Vazcaínos would win the Carioca State Championship. Edmundo had been a revelation, dovetailing superbly with the mercurial Bebeto as his side finished third in the Brasileirão, but his strong personality led to continued clashes with his teammates.

The previous 17 years had been a disaster for Palmeiras fans. They had watched on trophyless as Corinthians and São Paulo won their first national and international titles respectively. In 1992, however, they would be rescued by the investment of the multinational conglomerate Parmalat.

With Verdão surging thanks to Italian capital, coach Vanderlei Luxemburgo set about building one of the finest teams in Brazilian football history. Roberto Carlos, César Sampaio and Rivaldo were bright-eyed wunderkinds, but it was the capture of Edmundo for a record fee of $2m that captured fans’ imaginations. Vasco president Eurico Miranda was less than magnanimous, suggesting he was glad to get rid of a player who had been “a problem” for the dressing room.

Nevertheless, Edmundo would lead his new side to two straight Brasileirão titles and a State Championship. But “O Animal”, as he was christened by commentator Osmar Santos, once again found time to marry triumph with treachery. On 30 October 1994, São Paulo hosted Palmeiras at the Morumbi.

Like any Paulistano derby, it was a hot-blooded encounter, but both sides were resigned to a draw as the minutes ticked down. That was before Edmundo was on the receiving end of a particularly dodgy tackle near the touchline. Incensed, he raged at São Paulo coach Telê Santana on the bench, before seeking his retribution against striker Euller moments later.

A scrum ensued, with Edmundo punching André Luiz and slapping Juninho Paulista, prompting a full-scale fight between the teams in the process. By the time his teammate Antônio Carlos dragged him into the tunnel, six players had been sent off. Edmundo scored both his side’s goals that day, but nobody remembers them.

It wasn’t the only sour note. The year before, he had been given a 40-day suspension for pushing a referee in the face, whilst he also found time to get into a fistfight with Antônio Carlos, the very man who had rescued him from the ravenous São Paulo players. Repeated fallouts with Luxembergo, meanwhile, were par for the course. Five red cards in one season spoke of a man seemingly incapable of self-restraint.

In 1995, he would even be detained by Ecuadorian police, his frustration at missing a penalty in the Copa Libertadores causing him to kick out at a local cameraman. It was only with the intervention of the Brazilian government that his release from the country was negotiated.

Despite winning everything with Palmeiras, the allure of Rio always held sway for Edmundo. In 1995, he joined a club that boasted 15 per cent of the country’s population as fans. Flamengo wanted to build an “attack of dreams”, with Dinho starting alongside Romário and Sávio as the club set their sights on continental domination.

Unfortunately they didn’t know how to defend, a leaky defence and problems off the field scuppering their chances. A terrible year was summed up in the most brutal of fashions when, during the 1995 Supercopa Sudamericana against Vélez Sarsfield, Edmundo was knocked out cold by a vicious punch from Flavio Zandoná. Except for Palmeiras fans, hardly anybody was sympathetic.

Off the field, Edmundo had endured a nightmare, but on 2 December 1995, his life descended into hell. After partying in a nightclub during the carnival, an inebriated Edmundo got into his Jeep Cherokee before driving straight into a Fiat Uno in the Lagoa suburb of Rio. The car, which had been travelling at 60mph in a 40mph zone, careened straight into a telephone pole. All three passengers died from their injuries.

A tearful Edmundo was charged with involuntary manslaughter, whilst Flamengo tore up his contract. Not only did he face a possible jail sentence, but he also found himself without the one thing that had been constant in his life: football.

It would be Corinthians who offered him hope just 45 days later. As Edmundo’s lawyers interceded on his behalf, his attempts to concentrate on football hit an immediate snag, with the striker walking out on the club before he had made a single appearance. Eurico Miranda, the man who had greeted his departure from Vasco with such disdain years earlier, successfully sought to bring him back home.

It was the best season of Edmundo’s career, as he broke the Brazilian scoring record with 29 strikes. His form was so impressive that some argued for his inclusion as a starter over Ronaldo for the 1998 World Cup, but coach Mário Zagallo resisted, citing his disruptive influence on the squad.

Despite a last-minute change of heart that saw him included in the final selection, Zagallo would be proven right. Edmundo would spend the entire tournament complaining about a lack of minutes, even contacting a Rio radio station to air his frustration publicly. When Ronaldo suffered a seizure before the final in Paris, Edmundo seemed to have finally been given his chance, only for the young superstar to emerge for the game amidst accusations of cover-ups and veiled suggestions of conspiracy.

No matter. His 38 goals in 44 games had piqued Fiorentina owner Vittorio Cecchi Gori’s attention, and Edmundo was brought to Florence to augment one of Serie A’s most fearsome attacks. Alongside Rui Costa and Gabriel Batistuta, Edmundo would be charged with bringing domestic and European glory to La Viola. More importantly, though, it was a fresh start a thousand miles away from the flashbulbs and straplines of his home country.

Things went well at first, with the Brazilian combining lethally with Batistuta to fire his club to the top of Serie A. By the time Milan visited the Artemio Franchi in February, the home side had a chance to cement their lead, before Batistuta collapsed to the turf with an injury that would rule him out for two months.

Any normal footballer would have assumed the goalscoring mantle. Any footballer except for Edmundo would have been focused on delivering his team’s first Scudetto in 30 years. The Brazilian, however, was nowhere to be seen, having exercised a clause in his contract that allowed him to attend the Rio carnival back home.

Batistuta, like most of his teammates and the supporters, was incensed. “He was the right man if anyone wanted to have fun,” admitted the Argentine. “But to win something, he was not right.” By the time Edmundo returned to the club, his strikerless teammates had surrendered their lead, and would finish 14 points behind Lazio in third.

In each of his 18 months on the peninsula, Edmundo had made clear his desire to return home. When Eurico Miranda and Vasco called for him a third time, the transfer was as good as done. Back at his boyhood club and with the love of the fans behind him, Edmundo regained something close to his best form. The arrival at the club of Romário six months before the 2000 World Club Championship, however, reopened old wounds.

The pair had been friends until 1998, before falling out after Romário’s beach bar in Rio was found to contain a derisory painting of Edmundo on one of the bathrooms stalls. When Romário refused to take it down, the pair fell out in spectacular fashion, so much so that when he joined Vasco, their relationship became a massive media circus. Their feud has been covered in excruciating detail in Brazil and beyond; suffice to say, these two giant talents and their commensurate egos found cohabitation difficult.

Even the intercession of Vasco’s own priest, Padre Lino, couldn’t resolve their differences – not that Sir Alex Ferguson would have noticed. Romário and Edmundo combined with brutal efficiency to annihilate Manchester United in January 2000. After setting up Baixinho for the first, Edmundo had watched his partner capitalise on a second Gary Neville error to put the Brazilians two goals up.

On 43 minutes, Edmundo joined in himself, scoring a goal that summed up everything about what made him a special, irascible talent. Receiving an innocuous ball from Gilberto on the edge of the box, Vasco’s number 7 spun Mikaël Silvestre with the outside of his right boot, before sliding a finish past a hapless Mark Bosnich.

It was a moment of pure relief. Three months earlier, Edmundo had been strongly criticised by animal rights campaigners, after he was pictured giving beer and whiskey to a chimpanzee at his son’s first birthday party. He’d also spent a night in jail as a result of his ongoing trial, before his lawyers intervened to appeal. If he was trying to stay out of the headlines he was doing a very bad job of it, but the goal against United ensured he would finally be making waves for the right reason. It proved to be a brief respite.

The “worst moment” of Edmundo’s career would arrive in the final of the same tournament, his missed penalty consigning Vasco to the runners-up medal at the hands of Corinthians. It was his last meaningful contribution at the highest level.

Brief but tumultuous spells at eight clubs – including a further two stints at Vasco and another at Palmeiras – followed, but Edmundo failed to recapture the violent genius that had been his unmistakable trademark.

More tragedy would befall him in 2002, when his brother was found murdered in the back of his car in Rio. By the time the body was found, it was already in an advanced state of decomposition. Edmundo, overcome with grief, couldn’t bear to attend the funeral.

In 2011, the shadow that had hung over Edmundo’s life for 16 years was lifted. Magistrate Joaquim Barbosa ruled that, in the case of the fatal car crash that had claimed three lives, the statute of limitations had expired. Edmundo was free, but the grief of the moment still lives with him every day. “I am an eternal repentant,” he admitted in an interview with Brazilian media. “This sadness does not pass.”

There is no doubt that Edmundo’s career, with its litany of violent indiscretions and scurrilous headlines, makes less than pretty reading. But is he really, as one Brazilian journalist put it, “a liability to mankind”, or is he simply a deeply flawed human being, a man who struggled to reconcile a blessed gift with a cursed temperament? It’s a question that foregoes a simple answer. But what is simple is that Edmundo Alves de Souza Neto remains one of his country’s greatest talents. On the pitch at least, he is unassailable.

#2458. NBA Power Rankings: The LaMelo Ball effect is being felt in two places; Lakers take top spot from Spurs

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

When Timberwolves star Anthony Edwards went down after four games, I ranked it as the biggest injury blow any team has suffered this season, which was saying a lot given all the injuries we've seen. As it turned out, Oklahoma City's barrage of injuries, Kawhi Leonard in Toronto, Tyrese Haliburton in Indiana, Jaren Jackson Jr. in Utah, Paolo Banchero in Orlando, and now Stephen Curry with the Warriors have all turned out to be significantly more debilitating as Minnesota has gone 8-3 without Edwards.

How are they doing it? Let's take a look.

And by elite, we mean the best in the league. Minnesota is surrendering just 104 points per 100 possessions. Give Rudy Gobert his flowers, man. The Wolves' defensive rating drops to 97 points per 100 when he's on the court, while rising to 108.6 when he sits. That said, the Wolves have defenders everywhere you look and they are seriously tied together.

With their four regular starters on the floor (LaMelo Ball, Jaden McDaniels, Jonathan Kuminga and Gobert), Minnesota is registering a 92.0 defensive rating with a plus-20.5 net rating. But even when they go smaller and swap in Ayo Dosunmu for Gobert with the other three, the rating stays at 94.2 with a plus-16.2 net.

No matter the combination, if four of those five guys are on the court, the defense is no worse than 96.0. It's super impressive stuff, and so much for the idea that Ball is a defensive liability. Speaking of Ball ...

The LaMelo effect is being felt in two places: Minnesota, of course, but also Charlotte, where the offense has plummeted from a 123.3 rating with Ball on the court last year to a league-worst 103.1 this season. Being down Kon Knueppel doesn't help, but it's night and day watching this unit try to generate clean looks without Ball's creation and passing.

Meanwhile, the Wolves are flying. The defense is carrying the day and we're going to get to some of the guys carrying more impressive statistical weight than Ball, at least relatively, but watch this team play and try to argue his impact isn't all over the floor. He won the game for Minnesota on Tuesday with two defensive plays over the closing seconds.

LaMelo wins the game with back to back defensive plays! Who would have thought? 👀 pic.twitter.com/v9xYpR7eZu

Of course, his impact is felt most offensively. The pace. Energy. All of Minnesota's shooting percentages go up with Ball on the court, as they did last season in Charlotte, and that's not because of Ball's own shooting. He's only making 41.8% of his own shots, after all. It's his passing, his flow. As fancy as it is, it's fundamental in its contagious, force-multiplying impact.

The bottom line is this: Over his last 53 games between Charlotte and Minnesota, Ball has gone 39-14. That's the pace of a 60-win team. He's an agent of chaos, fine. It can look out of control. He still chucks up the playground shots, often off one foot and from barely inside the boundary. But we all wondered what it would look like when he was playing for a team with real stakes. Is he a winner? Or are his stats empty? Honestly, he's not even that impressive of a stats guy so far. He's just a winner.

The Wolves can deploy uncompromised lineups up and down their roster, meaning they don't have to decide between offense and defense. All their guys do both. They also have multiple offensive weapons even without Edwards, which is why Ball isn't having to carry a bigger scoring burden than he's equipped to handle, at least efficiently.

Terrence Shannon Jr. put up 34 off the bench in a win over Portland on Monday. The next night, Dosunmu and McDaniels, who are playing at legit All-Star levels, combined for 52 with nine 3-pointers. Kuminga is giving them 12.8 points, 5.7 rebounds, almost three assists and a steal over 30 minutes per game.

Other than Gobert, Jaylen Clark is really the only truly offensively limited guy, but for the minutes he gets, he is one hell of a defender. You do not want this man guarding you. You do not want anything to do with this team overall.

They came out of the gate looking incredible with Edwards and Ball looking like basketball brothers. It seemed like that was going to die out when Edwards got hurt. It hasn't.

When Edwards gets back, this Timberwolves team has the look of a legitimate contender.

#2457. Cowboys' handling of DC Christian Parker is bizarre, leaving Dallas with more questions than answers

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

FRISCO, Texas -- The Dallas Cowboys have always operated a little bit differently than the NFL's 31 other teams, mainly thanks to vocal owner Jerry Jones, who doubles as the team's general manager. However, the team's handling of first-year defensive coordinator Christian Parker amid a rough 4-6 start to the 2026 season may be one of the most downright bizarre decisions the Cowboys have made since Jones took over the team in 1989.

Jones floated that Dallas was "talking about" making a change at defensive coordinator on Tuesday after the Cowboys' 46-40 home defeat against the San Francisco 49ers in Week 10. That was understandable after Dallas allowed the 49ers to rack up 584 total yards, the most allowed in a Cowboys' home game in the 67-season history of the franchise. In the aftermath of another confounding defensive effort, the Cowboys now have the NFL's worst total defense (393.8 total yards per game allowed), run defense (154.1 rushing yards per game allowed), third down defense (48.8% third down conversion rate allowed) and the worst defense in terms of defensive expected points added (EPA) per play (-0.13).

Instead of firing Parker on Wednesday, which the team perhaps seemed primed to do, head coach Brian Schottenheimer announced senior defensive assistant Mike Pettine will call the defensive plays for the rest of the 2026 season. However, he won't become the team's new defensive coordinator. Yes, Parker, who, at 34 years old, is the youngest defensive coordinator in Cowboys' history, will remain the team's defensive coordinator and lead team meetings, but he has been stripped of play-calling responsibilities.

"I want to clarify a couple things right off the bat. Christian Parker is still our defensive coordinator," Schottenheimer said Wednesday. "He's a critical piece of what we're trying to do as we search for answers and solutions. And I think he has an incredibly bright future, not just this year, but beyond with us."

Building out the game plan and then calling it on game days is the bulk of an NFL defensive coordinator's job, but Schottenheimer has effectively neutered his developing DC. It's odd, which is why he felt he needed to reiterate multiple times that Parker's future remains in Dallas.

"I think I made it very clear that I see his future here. I see his future as our defensive coordinator. I do support him, but I do feel like based on where we stand today, that a different perspective was needed," Schottenheimer said.

So why make such a shake-up halfway through the season if the plays and the scheme won't be changing and Schottenheimer insists Parker's future is bright? Because Schottenheimer likely decided this is his last shot at being an NFL head coach, with his job status perhaps riding on the Cowboys' ability to win a depleted NFC East and reach the postseason. He wanted to go down with Pettine, a 60-year-old who was retired from coaching just a few months ago. Schottenheimer chose the man with 10 seasons of experience as either an NFL defensive coordinator (eight) or an NFL head coach (two).

"It's the different perspective," Schottenheimer said. "I think when you look at it, there's different ways to call plays. Pet's done this for a long time, but I want to be very clear. Play calling is a very collaborative thing. [Offensive coordinator] Klayton Adams, and I talk constantly...It's very collaborative. So I think that that's an important piece of it."

So what will Parker do now that he is no longer Dallas' defensive play caller? Still be the Cowboys' defensive coordinator despite now lacking one of the job's key responsibilities: play-calling. Schottenheimer said Parker will still run meetings and lead walkthroughs. Just "the only thing that's different is he's not calling the plays on game day."

Schottenheimer inferred Parker initially pushed back on the arrangement, answering that question with "we had a lot of conversations about different things."

So how does Parker get his play-calling responsibilities back in Dallas? The Cowboys head coach left that question unanswered.

The whole setup is bizarre, and the way Schottenheimer talks about Parker having a "very bright future here as our defensive coordinator" comes off like he is talking about a first-round-pick quarterback he has to bench because the speed of the game is too fast.

Take, for example, the Carolina Panthers, who benched 2023 first-overall-pick Bryce Young after the first two games of his second NFL season in 2024. He didn't get a chance to start again until Week 8 of that year. Young has since been a much better quarterback for the defending NFC South champions and current division leaders, but there really isn't a parallel to that in the coaching world.

"I've been around players that they get put on the bench for different reasons and things like that. But again, I don't see that with Christian," Schottenheimer said. "I don't think Christian Parker's being put on the bench. I think we're adjusting who's calling the plays on game day."

The closest comparison to this situation is when a young Sean Payton had offensive play-calling duties taken away from him as the New York Giants offensive coordinator in 2002. The Giants earned a wild card spot and lost in the opening round of the playoffs that year, 39-38, to the 49ers. Payton got another chance to call plays the next season, but it was on a new team — the Cowboys, ironically. Schottenheimer positioning this move as something that will make him, Parker, and the Cowboys stronger together is more wishful thinking than likely to come to fruition.

To be fair to Dallas' coaching staff, many of the issues the last few years have been with the players on the field. Per CBS Sports Research, the Cowboys are the only team in NFL history to allow 27-plus points per game in three consecutive seasons with a different defensive coordinator each year: Mike Zimmer (2024), Matt Eberflus (2025) and now Parker (2026). Nothing has stuck, which likely has more to do with Jones' roster-building and decision to trade away All-Pro edge rusher Micah Parsons to the Green Bay Packers. But, either way, Jones' and Schottenheimer's handling of Parker is very weird.

So what was the message to the Cowboys players who have to deal with this awkward situation? Parker is the defensive coordinator and the leader of the defense. He just won't do the most important job that a defensive coordinator does.

"I was upfront and honest with them," Schottenheimer said.

Being honest, though, would mean admitting this is a last-ditch effort to save a woeful defensive squad that has once again failed to live up to expectations.

Three-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle Kenny Clark is in his 11th NFL season, but he's never seen anything like this. He worked with both Parker and Pettine in Green Bay, but fresh off the practice field on Wednesday, he made it clear how saddened he is for Parker.

"I'm just bummed for CP for sure. I got a lot of respect for CP, and we're close," Clark said. "Bummed for sure, but the main thing is that we're all in this together."

Rookie safety Caleb Downs, the 11th overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, has probably spent more time with Parker than anyone else since he was drafted at the end of April. The two regularly meet one-on-one in Parker's offense to go over technique, communication and other coaching points. That's why hearing the news from Schottenheimer on Wednesday especially hurt Downs.

Both he and Clark spoke about Parker as if he was fired, even though he is still on staff. After all, that is basically what happened.

"It honestly hurt my heart; he's still our DC. He's somebody that we're playing for in the building and somebody that we love," Downs said Wednesday. "He's still in the building. He's still in the meetings. We still talk to him every day...Still someone we're looking to play for as one of our sources of motivation."

Why does it hurt? Because Parker built his secondary with the vision of a versatile chess piece in the mold of All-Pro Eagles defensive back Cooper DeJean, whom Parker worked with the last two seasons as Philadelphia's defensive passing game coordinator.

But how can this change help? Clark was initially at a loss for words, as most people likely are when trying to understand why the Cowboys are handling their defensive coordinator position the way that they are. Wednesday's decision to live in limbo with Parker is the latest in a series of missteps with Dallas' defense that began with the choice not to extend Parsons.

"I mean, uh I mean, we'll see. We'll see," Clark said. "Coach Pettine is a great coach. We're going to be running and doing the same things that we've been doing... It's no magic play call that Pet is going to be able to give us. It's our job to go out there and execute the game plan, whatever it is."

Whatever it is, it was an odd way to get there.
